What did Second International theorists do when confronted with the state’s relation to proletarian revolution?

They evaded it. Lenin's answer in *The State and Revolution* is that the Second International's leading theoreticians either ignored the question of the state's relation to proletarian revolution or, when directly confronted with it, dodged it — and this evasion was inseparable from the growth of opportunism:

> "The question of the relation of the state to the social revolution, and of the social revolution to the state, like the question of revolution generally, was given very little attention by the leading theoreticians and publicists of the Second International (1889-1914). But the most characteristic thing about the process of the gradual growth of opportunism that led to the collapse of the Second International in 1914 is the fact that even when these people were squarely faced with this question they tried to evade it or ignored it." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)

He generalizes the consequence:

> "In general, it may be said that evasiveness over the question of the relation of the proletarian revolution to the state--an evasiveness which benefited and fostered opportunism--resulted in the distortion of Marxism and in its complete vulgarization." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)

The chapter illustrates this with Plekhanov's *Anarchism and Socialism* (1894), which "contrived completely to evade the most urgent, burning, and most politically essential issue in the struggle against anarchism, namely, the relation of the revolution to the state, and the question of the state in general," instead substituting "a clumsy dissertation on the theme that an anarchist cannot be distinguished from a bandit." Lenin adds why the silence mattered:

> "For what opportunism needs most of all is that the two questions just mentioned should not be raised at all. That in itself is a victory for opportunism." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)

The chapter's second section, on Kautsky, then examines the same evasion in Kautsky's polemics against the opportunists. (All quotations are from the retrieved passage; broader historical context on the Second International is not in this excerpt.)

How do instructions to act justly compare with stories as ways to teach a lesson?

They operate differently: the justice passage teaches through **direct command and warning**, while the story teaches through **indirect analogy and inference**.

The Quran’s instruction is explicit and universal:

> “Be steadfast maintainers of justice, witnesses for God, though it be against yourselves, or your parents and kinsfolk, and whether it be someone rich or poor, for God is nearer unto both. So follow not your caprice, that you may act justly. If you distort or turn away, truly God is Aware of whatsoever you do.” (The Study Quran · Page 461)

Here the lesson is imposed as an obligation, with no need for a character or plot. It addresses the will directly and attaches accountability: God sees whether you distort or turn away.

In *Chapterhouse Dune*, Idaho teaches through story:

> “In one of my lives I had a dog that hated clams… He dug up the offender and brought it to me.” Idaho grinned. “Lesson one: Don’t let the unknown spit in your eye.” (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 20)

He then offers a second framing:

> “But look at it from the dog’s viewpoint. Go after the spitter! Then—glorious reward: Master is pleased.” (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 20)

The story works because Teg draws the application himself:

> “Do the Sisters think of us as dogs?”
> “In a way. Never forget it.” (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 20)

But the passage immediately moves from story back to direct instruction:

> “We’ve wasted enough time on stories! Let me see if your body has learned anything.” (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 20)

So the two are complementary: the story reshapes perspective and lets the listener discover a lesson, while the direct justice command prescribes required conduct and warns of consequences.

What does this commentary reveal about Lucilla’s inner conflict under the Honored Matre’s menace?

Her conflict is between two opposing survival imperatives: a personal wish to stop enduring and the collective Bene Gesserit memory inside her that insists she must — held together by a performance she knows is leaking.

**(1) The temptation to provoke her own death.** Her first move is suicidal candor:
> "It was tempting to prod this Honored Matre and evoke the dramatic response. Alarm her enough and she would certainly kill." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 12)

**(2) The Other Memories resist from within**, addressing her as one of them and begging the opposite:
> "Please, Sister! the Lampadas horde begged. Endure." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 12)

Her despair answers them — "You think I can escape from this place? That silenced them, except for one faint protest" — and the remnant answers back with the resilience maxim (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 12):
> "Remember! We are the ancient doll: seven times down, eight times up."

**(3) She reads her own situation as terminal** — "She's playing with me, Lucilla thought. She intends to kill me and feed me to her pet" — yet the horde keeps converting her observations into a reason to live: "But think of the tactical information you could provide if we did escape!" Her reply exposes the fracture exactly: "We! But there was no avoiding the accuracy of that protest" (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 12). She is simultaneously the woman in the cage and the chorus in it, and the "we" she resists is also the argument that keeps her alive.

**(4) The mask is the conflict's visible symptom.** Told in effect that Voice is her only resource, she thinks, "No Voice, eh? She thinks that's my only resource?" — then hides capability behind chit-chat and vulgarity, of which the narrator says: "Apparently no one had ever warned her to beware of the Bene Gesserit when they resorted to vulgarity. How do rational calculation and visionary experience differ in the kind of truth they reveal?

Rational calculation and visionary experience reveal different kinds of truth in these passages.

The Mentat Bashar Teg’s calculation is a structured, testable inference from observed facts. He notices details—banking houses, wealth, hidden observers—and moves from pattern to strategic conclusion:

> “A Prime Pattern development did not come into Teg’s mind but he had enough for a Testing Projection. Wealth not of this universe. People from the Scattering.” (Heretics of Dune · Chapter 12)

His truth is external and actionable: who is watching, what forces are present, what options exist.

Alia’s spice vision, by contrast, reveals time and destiny not as a chain of causes but as overwhelming, nonlinear experience:

> “Words … words. I can’t explain it. One thing is the occasion of another thing, but there’s no cause … no effect. We can’t leave the universe as it was. Try as we may, there’s a gap.” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 21)

She also finds that the vision lacks the stable object-quality that ordinary calculation depends on:

> “It has no thing-aspect. You can’t get under it or around it. There’s no place to get leverage.” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 21)

Under that visionary pressure, the truth she receives is personal and fate-like rather than strategic. She sees Duncan Idaho not as a tactical factor but as meaning itself:

> “He is the crucible, she thought. He is danger and salvation.” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 21)

So the difference is in kind: Teg’s Mentat calculation yields ordered, testable truth about the outer situation, while Alia’s vision yields direct but unstable truth about time, fate, and personal significance.

The evidence is narrative rather than editorial commentary, but it settles the point: Odrade's Convocation is presented as nearly unprecedented in Bene Gesserit history and freighted with the order's survival.

On rarity, the text says outright:

> "The last Convocation of the Bene Gesserit had been at the Tyrant's death. And before that, at the Tyrant's seizure of power. A Convocation had not been thought possible since Honored Matres attacked. Too much time taken from desperate labors." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 34)

Only two prior Convocations are named, and none has been considered feasible since the Honored Matres' assault. The scale of the risk is echoed when Bellonda asks whether Odrade will gather Sisters from scattered Keeps: > "Will you risk bringing Sisters from our surviving Keeps?" (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 34) and Odrade replies, > "Agreed. That is why I call Convocation." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 34). A natural phenomenon cannot be understood in isolation because, according to the dialectical method, every phenomenon is conditioned by its connection to surrounding phenomena. The evidence states:

> “The dialectical method therefore holds that no phenomenon in nature can be understood if taken by itself, isolated from surrounding phenomena, inasmuch as any phenomenon in any realm of nature may become meaningless to us if it is not considered in connection with the surrounding conditions, but divorced from them; and that, vice versa, any phenomenon can be understood and explained if considered in its inseparable connection with surrounding phenomena, as one conditioned by surrounding phenomena.” (Stalin · Dialectical and Historical Materialism)

Why did Western Europe and Japan build postwar agricultural support behind trade controls?

The library's answer is that those systems grew up behind — and in some cases were created by — the exchange and trade controls that had been imposed for balance-of-payments reasons, and that they were a copy of America's own farm policies:

> "much of Western Europe's and Japan's postwar systems of agricultural support and protection was built up behind, or even by means of, trade controls originally imposed on balance-of-payments grounds. These trade controls were discriminatory against U.S. exports, but they were simply an emulation of America's own agricultural practices." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 10)

Hudson adds that the controls were not free-standing protectionism: they were authorized under the GATT's balance-of-payments exceptions, and the agricultural support was layered onto them. He notes that Article XIII required quantitative restrictions to be nondiscriminatory, while Article XVIII was the infant-industry clause acknowledging that less developed countries needed to develop industries that free-trade rules would otherwise stifle (Super Imperialism · Chapter 10). So the legal architecture itself gave cover for the controls.

The political flashpoint was the U.S. demand for a permanent share of European food markets:

> "U.S. representatives demanded that American farmers be guaranteed a constant share of the British and Common Market grain markets. The United States would be made a guaranteed supplier of grains to Europe, crowding out Canada, Australia, Argentina and other agricultural exporters - and European farmers themselves. U.S. fruits and other products were to be similarly privileged. Continental Europe refused to concede this perpetual share of its food market." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 10)

That refusal mattered: Britain accepted the American proposal for its own market, and this "became a major problem blocking its entry into the European Community" (Super Imperialism · Chapter 10).

Context (not from the library): the standard historical reading is that wartime and immediate postwar dollar shortages forced Europe and Japan to ration scarce foreign exchange, and farm support was folded into that machinery rather than built separately — which is consistent with the Hudson passage, but the causal detail beyond it is general background rather than library text.

Why does Lady Jessica say Duncan and the other men have turned to heavy drinking?

**Short answer:** because they have lost their home — Caladan — and have not yet accepted Arrakis as one, and they are losing faith in the Duke.

In the conversation with Thufir Hawat, Jessica reads the drinking as a symptom rather than a discipline problem:

> "Apply your Mentat abilities to it!" she snapped. "What's the problem with Duncan and the others? I can tell you in four words—they have no home." (Dune · Chapter 17)

When Hawat objects that Arrakis is their home, she rejects that outright:

> "Arrakis is an unknown! Caladan was their home, but we've uprooted them. They have no home. And they fear the Duke's failing them." (Dune · Chapter 17)

So the heavy consumption of spice beer by Duncan Idaho and the others is, in her diagnosis, the visible symptom of displacement and eroded confidence: Hawat has reports that Idaho "overindulged in something called spice beer" and that others "have been stupefied by this concoction" (Dune · Chapter 17). Jessica's framing is explicitly medical — "Is it defeatist or treacherous for a doctor to diagnose a disease correctly? My only intention is to cure the disease" (Dune · Chapter 17) — i.e., the drinking is not treason or mere idleness, but the sign of men unmoored from place and trust.

Note (context, not a quotation): this is the same theme she states more generally later in the scene — destroy a person's place and you destroy the person (Dune · Chapter 17).

What does the commentary suggest about Hwi’s calm composure and Moneo’s hidden unease?

The passage is Herbert's narrative voice rather than a separate critical commentary, and it frames the contrast as a study in composure versus concealment: Hwi's calm is genuine and self-possessed, while Moneo's unease is visible only to those who can read what he tries to hide.

**Hwi's composure.** She "appeared calm as she approached Leto and sat without being invited, choosing a golden cushion rather than the red one she had occupied earlier." (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28) Her calm is not passivity — she has already registered Moneo's disturbance and turns it into a question: "Something has disturbed Moneo... He tried very hard not to reveal this to me, but the more he tried to soothe me the more he aroused my curiosity." (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28) She is described as having "an immovable core of self-honesty" that defeats her Bene Gesserit teachers' conditioning — "Everything strengthening that power which prevented her from becoming a Bene Gesserit." (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28)

**Moneo's hidden unease.** His agitation is physical and involuntary: "Leto's acute hearing detected Moneo fidgeting in the anteroom and Leto sent a signal which sealed the arched doorway there." (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28) So the concealment is deliberate but imperfect — Moneo's overcompensation ("the more he tried to soothe me") is exactly what betrays him. What he was brooding on is the observation Hwi reports: "He said that I must remember it at all times, that the God Leto is a different person to each of us," adding that Moneo "often wonders what part we play in creating that difference in you." (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28) Hwi judges this "a truthful insight," and Leto agrees: "That is interesting." (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28)

The implied reading: Hwi's stillness is the composure of honesty, while Moneo's fidgeting is the anxiety of a courtier managing a truth he can't fully voice — and Hwi's calm is what makes that anxiety legible.

Why did the postwar inter-governmental debt system prove so damaging?

The damage came from a structural mismatch: the debts were inter-governmental paper claims with no productive counterpart, and the debtor nations had no realistic way to earn the dollars to service them.

Hudson's central diagnosis (note: the scanned text runs two columns together, so the sentence is interleaved but intact):

> "The destructive éffect of the postwar inter-governmental debt system was aggravated by the fact that its financial claims had no counterpart in productive capital resources, leaving no real means by which it might be paid. It was rather a calculation of the cost of destroying Europe's resources." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2)

Keynes is invoked to break the false analogy between private productive lending and inter-governmental claims — the typical bankers' view being:

> "that a comparable system between Governments, on a far vaster and definitely oppressive scale, represented by no real assets, and less closely associated with the property system, is natural and reasonable and in conformity with human nature." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2)

An old country could develop a young country by private investment because "the arrangement may be mutually advantageous, and out of abundant profits the lender may hope to be repaid. But the position cannot be reversed." Hence:

> "A young country such as the United States could not expect the older countries of Europe to be capable of out-producing her to the extent of generating a salable export surplus sufficient to amortize the heavy Inter-Ally debts and at the same time to meet internal needs." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2)

And on issuing European bonds in America: "the analogy will be a false one; because, taken in the aggregate, there is no natural increase, no real sinking fund, out of which they" could be paid (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2).

Two aggravating factors are documented:

1. **U.S. protectionism blocked the transfer mechanism.** Washington "restored the high level of Import duties set by the Payne-Aldrich Act of 1909. Tariffs on dutiable imports were raised to an average 38 per cent, compared to 16 per cent in 1920." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2)

How do people respond to disruption—through rituals that restore social balance, or by growing formal and afraid?

Both responses appear in the evidence — and the contrast is precisely the point.

**Restoring balance.** Michael Hudson describes disruption met by ritual renewal of social equity, typically at a new year or new reign:

> "The idea was to renew not only nature but also social balance in general. The common denominator is to restore amity and equity in a celebratory setting." (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 10)

These ceremonies were practical as well as symbolic — debts were actually cancelled and prisoners released:

> "Many societies have released lawbreakers on such occasions. Europeans and Asians, African and Native Americans have long used the New Year as an occasion to clean their homes, bring their extended families together and put their economic relations in order, especially by settling debts." (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 10)

**Growing formal and afraid.** Dune shows the opposite reflex, in Jessica's reaction to her son Paul during their flight across the desert after the sandslide:

> "How stiffly formal I speak to my own son! Then, because it was the Bene Gesserit way to seek within for the answer to such an oddity, she searched and found the source of her formality: I'm afraid of my son; I fear his strangeness; I fear what he may see ahead of us, what he may tell me ." (Dune · Chapter 27)

Notably, her fear of disruption (their perilous escape) and of Paul's prescient strangeness produces stiffness rather than communal warmth; even her self-diagnosis is a trained, inward procedure rather than a restorative ceremony.

**So the evidence answers: it depends.** Hudson's collection of New Year and jubilee customs shows disruption routed into shared, celebratory redistribution — settling debts, reuniting families, releasing offenders. Dune's passage shows disruption routed into formality and fear, where intimacy curdles into caution and the "answer" is sought by solitary introspection, not collective ritual. The evidence does not, however, offer any passage that directly compares or adjudicates between the two responses — they come from separate books addressing separate subjects (ancient debt economics vs. a science-fiction flight scene), so the pairing is juxtaposition rather than an argued thesis.

How does divine oneness compare with New Year renewal as a source of harmony?

They are different but complementary kinds of harmony: divine oneness is an inward, spiritual harmony of the soul toward God, while New Year renewal is an outward, social harmony through resetting debts and restoring equity.

Divine oneness works by forming an inner habit of obedience and submission:

> “Such (declaration of the) oneness of God does not merely refer to faith, which is affirmation based upon judgment. The object of (all human) actions and divine worship is acquisition of the habit of obedience and submissiveness, and the freeing of the heart from all preoccupations save the worshipped Master, until the novice on the path to God becomes a holy person.” (The Muqaddimah · The Various Kinds of Sciences)

Its harmony becomes complete when faith controls conduct:

> “Thus, all actions, eventually, become subservient to this affirmation by faith, and this is the highest degree of faith. It is perfect faith. The believer who has it will commit neither a great nor a small sin.” (The Muqaddimah · The Various Kinds of Sciences)

New Year renewal, by contrast, restores social and economic balance:

> “The idea was to renew not only nature but also social balance in general. The common denominator is to restore amity and equity in a celebratory setting.” (Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 10)

It does this through debt settlement and family/community repair:

> “Europeans and Asians, African and Native Americans have long used the New Year as an occasion to clean their homes, bring their extended families together and put their economic relations in order, especially by settling debts.” (Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 10)

So divine oneness harmonizes the individual from within—freeing the heart and producing sinless obedience—while New Year renewal harmonizes the community from without—releasing lawbreakers, settling debts, and restoring amity and equity.

What is the difference between centralized state power and personal trust in uniting people?

The evidence does not directly address "personal trust" as a way of uniting people — that framing isn't in the retrieved passages. What it *does* contain is a distinction between **centralism as an organizational form** and **what that centralism rests on**: the old bureaucratic machine versus the voluntary union of armed workers.

Key points from the evidence:

- Centralism itself is not the issue — its class basis is:
> "Centralism is possible with both the old and the new state machine." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)
- A unity of armed workers is still centralist, but rests on the destruction of the old apparatus rather than on it:
> "If the workers voluntarily unite their armed forces, this will be centralism, but it will be based on the 'complete destruction' of the centralized state apparatus—the standing army, the police, and the bureaucracy." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)
- The decisive difference is which machine the ruling class uses:
> "Revolution consists not in the new class commanding, governing with the aid of the old state machine, but in this class smashing this machine and commanding, governing with the aid of a new machine." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)
- The passage also argues that under capitalism officials tend to become "privileged persons divorced from the people and standing above the people," which is why formal office-holding (even elected office) is not the same as genuine unity from below.

**From general knowledge (paraphrase, not a quote from these sources):** centralized state power unites people *through* an apparatus — law, bureaucracy, police, army — which can compel coordination whether or not anyone trusts anyone. Personal trust unites people through voluntary relationships, shared commitment, and mutual confidence, with no coercive machinery behind it. The two can coincide (a voluntary federation can be centralized) or diverge (a centralized state may hold together a distrustful population by force). The evidence above supports the first half of that contrast; the "personal trust" half is not sourced in the retrieved material.

How do magical ability and socialist democracy differ in their sources of power and methods of practice?

The evidence does not support a full comparison, because it supplies a substantive account of magical ability but not of socialist democracy. The “Socialist Democracy in Practice” item is largely a bibliography, not an explanation of its power source or methods.

For magical ability, Ibn Khaldun describes its source and practice directly. He writes that magical souls are distinguished by a particular quality, and that ability is actualized through exercise:

> “The souls that have magical ability are of three degrees. These three degrees will now be explained here. The first kind exercises its influence merely through mental power, without any instrument or aid. This is what the philosophers call sorcery. The second kind exercises its influence with the aid of the temper of the spheres and the elements, or with the aid of the properties of numbers. This is called talismans. It is weaker in degree than the first kind. The third kind exercises its influence upon the powers of imagination…” (The Muqaddimah · p. 431)

Its method of practice is also specified:

> “All magical exercise consists of directing oneself to the spheres, the stars, the higher worlds, or to the devils by means of various kinds of veneration and worship and submissiveness and humiliation.” (The Muqaddimah · p. 431)

For socialist democracy, the provided evidence contains only references such as:

> “Leib, Ethan, and He Baogang (eds.). 2006. The search for deliberative democracy in China.” (Socialism_With_Chinese_Characteristics · Chapter 234)

It does not state how socialist democracy draws its power or how it is practiced. Therefore, from the evidence alone, a direct contrast cannot be made. From general knowledge, socialist democracy is ordinarily understood to derive authority from the people through party/state institutions and to operate through elections, consultation, legislation, and rule of law—not through an individual soul’s occult power, talismans, or manipulation of imagination; but that contrast is outside the provided evidence.

That line is on the book's front matter and is attributed to Herman Kahn in 1972, quoted as an admiring remark addressed to Hudson:

> "You've shown how the United States has run rings around Britain and every other empire-building nation in history. We've pulled off the greatest rip-off ever achieved." — Herman Kahn (1972) (Super Imperialism · Page 1)

> "In this book Michael Hudson illuminates one of the most powerful forces in global economics - one which is hidden, and widely misunderstood. This 'money-pump' works at almost no cost to Americans, and at considerable cost to those who pour dollars into the 'pump' - the rest of us. So the two ideas sit side by side in the front matter but have different authors: the "money-pump" description is Pettifor's; the "greatest rip-off ever achieved" is Kahn's. Why is dialectical materialism called dialectical materialism?

Dialectical materialism is called that because it combines a dialectical method with a materialist theory:

> “It is called dialectical materialism because its approach to the phenomena of nature, its method of studying and apprehending them, is dialectical, while its interpretation of the phenomena of nature, its conception of these phenomena, its theory, is materialistic.” (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · p. 1)

So “dialectical” refers to its method of understanding nature as connected, changing, and developing through contradictions; “materialism” refers to its view that material reality is primary and that ideas are reflections of the material world.

How is the hidden money-pump in global economics like carpentry's reliance on geometry?

The evidence does not explicitly compare the money-pump to carpentry, but it supports this analogy: both depend on a hidden structural mechanism. The money-pump is hidden and misunderstood, and carpentry depends on geometry’s invisible rules of proportion and measurement.

Hudson’s opening description calls the money-pump “hidden, and widely misunderstood” and says it “liberally pumps out money to finance extravagant U.S. consumption and spending.” It “works at almost no cost to Americans, and at considerable cost to those who pour dollars into the ‘pump’ — the rest of us” (Super Imperialism · p. 1). The hidden mechanism is that foreign central banks “simply add the surplus dollars to their reserves, mainly in the form of U.S. Treasury IOUs,” so “other countries monetary assets are thus America’s monetary debt” (Super Imperialism · p. 1).

Likewise, Ibn Khaldun writes that carpentry “needs a good deal of geometry of all kinds” and “requires either a general or a specialized knowledge of proportion and measurement, in order to bring forms from potentiality into actuality in the proper manner” (The Muqaddimah · On the various aspects of making a living). Just as the carpenter cannot bring a ship or joined structure into actuality without recourse to the geometrician, the money-pump cannot operate without the hidden architecture of dollar reserves and Treasury IOUs.

How do charitable giving and interest-free lending to kin compare as acts of faith?

The evidence does not directly compare the two, but each is presented as a commanded economic act of faith with a distinct emphasis.

Charitable giving in the Quran is paired with prayer and oriented toward the Day of Judgment:

> “Tell My servants who believe to perform the prayer and to spend from that which We have provided them, secretly and openly, before a day comes wherein there shall be neither bargaining nor befriending.” (The Study Quran · 14:31)

The commentary explains that this refers to the Day of Judgment, “when the ability to negotiate and appeal to friends for help will be of no avail” (The Study Quran · 14:31). So the act of spending is tied to eschatological urgency and accountability.

Interest-free lending to kin in Deuteronomy is framed as a covenantal duty within the community:

> “You shall not demand interest from your kindred on a loan of money or of food or of anything else which is loaned. From a foreigner you may demand interest, but you may not demand interest from your kindred, so that the Lord, your God, may bless you in all your undertakings on the land you are to enter and possess.” (The Catholic Study Bible · Deuteronomy 23:20–21)

Here the stated motive is blessing in the land, and the rule is specifically limited to “your kindred,” since interest may be demanded from a foreigner.

Thus, both practices express faith through the use of wealth: the Quranic command emphasizes generous spending as preparation for judgment, while the Deuteronomic command emphasizes kinship solidarity and covenant blessing.

How do public declarations of principle compare with dynastic calculations in shaping who governs?

**Short answer:** In the evidence, the two work on different currencies. Public declarations of principle make rule legitimate only through "the consent of the governed," while dynastic calculation treats rule as a bloodline inheritance to be defended, transferred, and arranged through secret plans.

**The Declaration: principle as the title to govern.** Aptheker argues the manifesto's novelty is that it grounds authority in the people's will, not rulers' claims:

> "This itself is new and reflects the essence of the Declaration's political philosophy—the sovereignty of the people." (Aptheker · The Declaration of Independence)

And that its logic is explicitly anti-dynastic:

> "Hierarchy is, then, rejected and with it aristocracy and monarchy and the divine right of ruler or rulers. Equality of man replaces it and therefore sovereignty lies with these equals, and it is their will which is divine, if anything is" (Aptheker · The Declaration of Independence)

The corollary is that principle generates a standing right of exit:

> "If to the above is added its logical corollary-that government must rest on 'the consent of the governed,' as the Declaration says—then the right of revolution is indubitable." (Aptheker · The Declaration of Independence)

Aptheker even denies that a republic dissolves this right: "the people must consent to being governed; if enough of them do not and if the grievances are sufficiently serious, the right of revolution is theirs." (Aptheker · The Declaration of Independence)

**Dune: dynastic calculation as the operative title.** The Harkonnen scene shows governance being shaped by succession logic rather than declared principle. The Baron uses a Mentat as a lesson for his heir — "Observe the plans within plans within plans." (Dune · Chapter 2) — and judges Feyd-Rautha by capacity to inherit: "He aspires to rule my Barony, yet he cannot rule himself." (Dune · Chapter 2) Feyd-Rautha reads the briefing as dynastic promotion: "The old monster is letting me in on secret things at last. He must really mean for me to be his heir." (Dune · Chapter 2) The objective is not consent but extinction of a rival line: "I must have him dead and his line ended." (Dune · Chapter 2) Loyalty itself is purchased, not principled — Piter's "pleasures are what tie you to me." (Dune · Chapter 2)

**The comparison.** Principle asks *whether* a people consents; dynasty asks *who* is next and how to secure it — Dune's "plans within plans" are exactly the secret arrangements Aptheker's Declaration would submit to "the opinion of mankind." The evidence presents these as opposing grounds of rule, though the two books never directly address each other.

So: freezing the principles would contradict their scientific status, block adaptation to concrete national conditions, and prevent the ongoing development Xi calls China's original contribution.

What is the key to understanding today's dollar standard?

The key is that the dollar standard is no longer a gold-based asset standard but a debt standard based on U.S. Treasury IOUs:

> “The key to understanding today's dollar standard is to see that it has become a debt standard based on U.S. Treasury IOUs, not on assets in the form of gold bullion.” (Super Imperialism · introductory matter)

According to the commentary, why can’t humans defend themselves without tools and other people?

Two reasons, both from Ibn Khaldūn's account of why social organization is natural and necessary to humans.

**1. Unaided human bodies lack natural weapons, and crafted weapons require many hands/crafts.** Humans compensate for their lack of natural defenses with artificial ones, but those must be made:

> "The crafts, in turn, procure for man the instruments that serve him instead of limbs, which other animals possess for their defence. Lances, for instance, take the place of horns for goring, swords the place of claws to inflict wounds, shields the place of thick skins, and so on." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1: "Human Civilization in General" · p. 46)

But no single person can supply those instruments:

> "The power of one individual human being cannot withstand the power of any one dumb animal, especially the power of the predatory animals. Man is generally unable to defend himself against them by himself. Nor is his unaided power sufficient to make use of the existing instruments of defence, because there are so many of them and they require so many crafts and things. It is absolutely necessary for man to have the co-operation of his fellow men." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1: "Human Civilization in General" · p. 46)

The consequence of that lack of cooperation is death before one's time:

> "Nor, lacking weapons, can he defend himself. Thus, he falls prey to animals and dies much before his time." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1: "Human Civilization in General" · p. 46)

**2. Weapons against animals do not suffice against other humans.** Because every person is armed alike, defence against human aggression must come from within the species — a restraining authority:

> "The weapons made for the defence of human beings against the aggressiveness of dumb animals do not suffice against the aggressiveness of man to man, because all of them possess those weapons. Thus, something else is needed for defence against the aggressiveness of human beings toward each other... This is the meaning of royal authority." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1: "Human Civilization in General" · p. 46)

**Summary (commentary-based):** solitary humans are physically weaker than predatory animals, their defensive tools are artificial and too numerous for one person to make, and even with tools they cannot guard against each other — hence cooperation, crafts, and political authority are all necessary for survival.

How do personal pride and international debt each influence financial prosperity?

Personal pride and international debt influence financial prosperity in opposite ways in the evidence: pride tends to destroy an individual’s livelihood, while international debt can enrich creditor nations but strain debtor nations.

On personal pride, Ibn Khaldun says proud people often cut themselves off from the rank and social cooperation that bring wealth:

> “many people who are proud and supercilious have no use for rank. Their earnings, consequently, are restricted to (the results of) their own labours, and they are reduced to poverty and indigence.” (The Muqaddimah · ON THE VARIOUS ASPECTS OF MAKING A LIVING)

He explains the mechanism: a haughty person expects deference, but people resent this and withhold kindness and access to higher ranks:

> “when a haughty person has no rank—and he cannot have any, as has been explained—people hate him for his haughtiness, and he receives no share of their kindness. He obtains no rank from members of the next higher class, because he is hated by them…” (The Muqaddimah · ON THE VARIOUS ASPECTS OF MAKING A LIVING)

The result is severe:

> “In consequence, his livelihood is destroyed. He remains in a state of indigence and poverty or of one only a little better. The acquisition of wealth is altogether out of the question for him.” (The Muqaddimah · ON THE VARIOUS ASPECTS OF MAKING A LIVING)

On international debt, Hudson describes a different dynamic in World War I finance. Debt allowed the United States to shift its international investment position and profit from arms sales, while allied debtor nations reached their financial limit:

> “That represented Europe’s financial limit in terms of normal commercial standards. The continent was close to the end of its financial tether by the time the United States entered the war. It lacked means to purchase American arms for cash in the amounts required, and lacked adequate collateral on which to borrow further sums through U.S. banks.” (Michael Hudson - Super Imperialism · Chapter 1)

The obligations built up massively:

> “obligations of the Allies to the United States Government grew to $12 billion by 1921” (Michael Hudson - Super Imperialism · Chapter 1)

And the shift away from subsidies toward loans had lasting costs:

> “When loans were granted in place of subsidies, they invited unfortunate consequences” (Michael Hudson - Super Imperialism · Chapter 1)

How does the commentary describe the ties between American and English radical movements before the Revolution?

The commentary frames the two movements as a single, mutually reinforcing transatlantic radical current, not two separate phenomena.

Its central claim: "The tie between the American and English radical movements is exemplified not only in the person of Thomas Paine, as is well known, but also by the career of John Wilkes, leader of the latter." (Aptheker, American Revolution · "England and the Revolution"). Wilkes' political correspondence with Americans "goes back at least to 1758, and in the 1760's and 1770's he was in fre-quent contact with American radicals, especially those active in the Boston Sons of Liberty," evidenced by a letter to him "signed by a 'Committee of the Sons of Liberty' of Boston (including John Adams, Joseph Warren and Benjamin Church) dated June 6, 1768" (Aptheker, American Revolution · "England and the Revolution").

The same page notes the "election of John Adams, in 1773, to member-ship in that same London Society," and "the raising of funds by the Constitutional Society in England, to help the widows and orphans of the Americans slain at Lexington and Concord, with a leader of this Society, John Horne Tooke, sentenced to jail for seditious libel" (Aptheker, American Revolution · "England and the Revolution") — showing the tie operating through organized societies, not merely personal friendships.

The commentary also presents the tie as propagandistic and literary: "It was the American effort, and the English effort, which together form the theme of mass-distributed pamphlets published in England, like Catherine Sawbridge Macaulay's Address to the People of England, Scotland, and Ireland… and John Cartwright's, American Independence, the Interest and Glory of Britain, both issued in 1775." (Aptheker, American Revolution · "England and the Revolution"). Welsh sympathizers are folded into the same current — Richard Price and David Williams, the latter "a friend of Franklin," who in 1782 published Letters on Personal Liberty defending "the American Revolutionists" while urging universal male suffrage, annual parliaments, and press freedom (Aptheker, American Revolution · "England and the Revolution").

Finally, the tie is shown working through municipal government: "It was the Aldermen and the Lord Mayor of London—John Wilkes… who petitioned the King in 1775 to dismiss the Ministers oppressing the colonies," arguing that "the liberties of the whole [Empire are] inevitably connected with those of every part." (Aptheker, American Revolution · "England and the Revolution").

In short, the commentary describes the link as personal (Paine, Wilkes), organizational (Sons of Liberty, Constitutional Society), literary (Macaulay, Cartwright, Jones), and civic (the London petition) — with English radicals treating American grievances as their own.

Why does Kautsky’s quotation about the Commune fail to address the real argument about centralism and the state?

**Short answer:** because Kautsky's quotation is about the *wrong question*. Lenin's charge in Chapter VI is that the real issue is not whether "centralism" or officials exist, but whether the *old state machine* is smashed and replaced — and Kautsky's borrowed quotation about the Commune never touches that.

**1. The quotation is irrelevant to the point at issue.** Lenin says outright: "Kautsky's 'quotation' is neither here nor there." He adds that "Kautsky acts like an outright swindler by evading the perfectly well-known arguments of Marx and Engels on the Commune and plucking out a quotation which has nothing to do with the point at issue." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)

**2. Centralism is not the disputed question.** Lenin's own formulation is that "Centralism is possible with both the old and the new state machine." Workers voluntarily uniting their armed forces would still be centralism — but "based on the 'complete destruction' of the centralized state apparatus—the standing army, the police, and the bureaucracy." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI) So a quotation defending centralism settles nothing: centralism can be built on the ruins of the old apparatus, not on its preservation.

**3. Kautsky substitutes "opposition" for "revolution."** By asking whether "our political struggle abolishes ... the state power before we have captured it," and by insisting "we are not discussing here the form the 'future state' will be given," Kautsky shifts ground: "By skipping to the question of 'opposition', Kautsky substitutes the opportunist for the revolutionary point of view... Revolution has vanished! And that is exactly what the opportunists wanted." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)

**4. His question about officials misses the Marxian lesson.** Kautsky's "We cannot do without officials even in the party and trade unions..." shows, for Lenin, that "he does not understand the lessons of the Commune or the teachings of Marx," since "We cannot do without officials under capitalism, under the rule of the bourgeoisie" — the corrupting pressure is capitalism, not administration as such (State and Revolution · Chapter VI).

**5. The real question is the machine, not the ministries.** "The point is not at all whether the 'ministries' will remain, or whether 'committees of specialists' or some other bodies will be set up; that is quite immaterial. The point is whether the old state machine ... shall remain, or be destroyed and replaced by a new one." Hence: "Revolution consists not in the new class commanding, governing with the aid of the old state machine, but in this class smashing this machine and commanding, governing with the aid of a new machine." (State and Revolution · Chapter VI)

How do close relationships across different groups reshape a people’s inherited wisdom and their family lines?

Cross-group intimacy does two opposite things at once: it dissolves the memory of descent (so family lines blur and merge), and it generalizes inherited wisdom into something any people can adopt — while at the same time undermining the group feeling that made leadership and nobility legitimate in the first place.

Ibn Khaldūn describes the first effect directly:

> "the original descent is almost forgotten. Those who knew about it have passed away, and it is no longer known to most people. Family lines in this manner continually changed from one tribal group to another, and some people developed close contact with others (of a different descent)." (The Muqaddimah · p. 139)

But he insists this blending cannot simply transfer authority, because "Leadership over people who share in a given group feeling cannot be vested in those not of the same descent" (The Muqaddimah · p. 139). The attached outsider "is merely attached to them. The firmest connection he has with the group is as client and ally" (The Muqaddimah · p. 139). Hence the paradox of the mixed line: those who are eager to acquire pedigrees "do not realize that they thus bring suspicion upon themselves with regard to their leadership and nobility" (The Muqaddimah · p. 139).

And inherited wisdom is preserved only where the group stays unmixed: "Wherever the group feeling is truly formidable and its soil kept pure, the advantage of a common descent is most evident, and the (group feeling) is more effective" (The Muqaddimah · p. 140). Sedentary mixing reverses it: "A 'house' possesses an original nobility through group feeling and personal qualities. Later on, the people (who have a 'house') divest themselves of that nobility when group feeling disappears as the result of sedentary life, and they mingle with the common people" (The Muqaddimah · p. 140). City dwellers, he adds, "can have a 'house' only in a metaphorical sense" (The Muqaddimah · p. 140).

Frank Herbert frames the other side — wisdom made portable. Fremen insight passes "In small pieces, bits and parcels which grow into general understanding, the Fremen racial wisdom is translated into a new certainty. The thing Fremen have as a people, any people can have" (Children of Dune · Chapter 56). Yet his Arrakis shows the same erosion Khaldūn feared: "The rural districts were colonies of the urban centers. They'd learned how to wear a padded yoke, led into it by their greed if not their superstitions" (Children of Dune · Chapter 56) — the old ways "reduced to ritual words, their origins lost to memory."

So: contact widens wisdom into a shared, teachable certainty, but it forgets lineage and dilutes the group feeling on which inherited rank depended.

That one is a squad leader. That one is a Captain General. This one is a lowly sergeant and here is a messenger.

How were the delegates to the Second Continental Congress selected, unlike the earlier Congress?

Delegates to the Second Continental Congress were chosen by the revolutionary congresses or conventions rather than by the regular provincial assemblies:

> "The delegates this time were selected not by provincial assemblies but rather by the revolutionary congresses or conventions already mentioned." (Aptheker · American Revolution · "The Development of Revolutionary Institutions")

Luke explains why, by grounding Jesus’s message in the Jubilee tradition. For many years Biblical scholarship interpreted his version as being an idiosyncratic elaboration of Mark 6: 1–6, perhaps drawing on non-Mark traditions. But discovery of the Dead Sea scrolls suggests that it was Mark and the other gospel writers who skipped over the significance of Jesus’ deror citation from Isaiah, and subsequent Christianity, not Jesus, that treated “release” as a metaphor for a more spiritualized advent of God’s reign and “forgiveness of humankind … a metaphor for God’s work of redemption and reconciliation.” [586]   For subsequent Christianity, the coming sovereignty of God was to end the old worldly order, rescuing “the poor” but not by taking the specific worldly policy of cancelling the debts that held them in poverty and stripped them of their land and means of self-support.

> Jesus’ Parable of the Unmerciful Servant (Matthew 18) leaves little doubt that the poor literally should be forgiven their debts. Admonishing Peter to excuse his brother’s sins, Jesus explains that admission to heaven depends on how one conducts his life in accordance with the principle of Leviticus 19: 18: “Love thy neighbor as thyself.” This precept forms the basis for the Golden Rule that we should not do unto others what we would not wish them to do unto us.
>
> Jesus’ parable applies this ethic to debt forgiveness. A king calls his officials and administrators together to settle accounts with them. The first man brought in is a satrap who owes him ten thousand talents. Unable to pay this enormous amount, he asks for more time to collect more taxes from his subjects. But the king orders that the insolvent satrap, his wife, children “and all that he had be sold to repay the debt. The satrap fell on his knees before him and begged, ‘Be patient with me and I will pay back everything.’ His master took pity on him, canceled the debt and let him go. But when that satrap went out, he found one of his subordinate officials who owed him a hundred denarii . He grabbed the official and began to choke him. ‘Pay back what you owe me!’ he demanded. His fellow royal servant fell to his knees and begged him, ‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you back.’” But the satrap refused, and had his subordinate thrown into prison until he could pay the debt.
>
> When the royal servants told the king what had happened, he called his satrap back. “‘You wicked servant,’ he said, ‘I canceled all that debt of yours because you begged me to. Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?’ In anger the king turned him over to the jailers until he should pay back all he owed.” Jesus warns: “This is how my heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.”

How does the commentary understand Jesus’s inaugural sermon—as a literal Jubilee release from debt, not merely spiritual freedom?

The commentary reads Jesus's inaugural sermon as a literal proclamation of the Jubilee—actual cancellation of debts and release of debt bondsmen—not a spiritualized metaphor.

Luke alone records the sermon; Hudson argues this is because Luke grounded it in the Jubilee tradition:

> "(Third) Isaiah 61, where the prophet (as noted above in Chapter 24) announces that the Lord has sent him 'to preach good news (gospel) to the poor' and 'to proclaim freedom (deror) for the prisoners and … to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor,' that is, the Jubilee Year. Jesus informed the congregation that he had come to fulfill that destiny. Treating debt bondage literally, not as merely a metaphor for spiritual bondage, Jesus the Redeemer set about preaching literal redemption from debt." (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 38)

He also notes the reversal of blame for the spiritualizing reading:

> "…subsequent Christianity, not Jesus, that treated 'release' as a metaphor for a more spiritualized advent of God's reign and 'forgiveness of humankind … a metaphor for God's work of redemption and reconciliation.'" (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 38)

The parable of the Unmerciful Servant (Matthew 18) clinches the literal reading: the king "canceled the debt and let him go," and the unforgiving satrap is jailed "until he should pay back all he owed" (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 38). The Lord's Prayer is likewise read as debt language: Matthew 6:12 reads "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors (tois opheiletais)," and on that ground Ringe calls it a "Jubilee Prayer" (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 38). Hudson adds Drake's two arguments—that the petition "incorporates human action into a prayer, and uses the language of debt," since only God can forgive sins, and that the Greek word means specifically monetary debts (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 38).

This sits against Hillel's prosbul clause, which let debts survive the sabbatical year; Luke 6:35's "lend, without expecting to be repaid" is "the opposite of the intent of Hillel's prosbul clause" (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 38).

Outside the library: this literalist Jubilee reading is Hudson's own economic-historical thesis, and mainstream NT scholarship often treats Isaiah 61 as typological/metaphorical rather than a program of actual debt cancellation.

What does this commentary say about communism making the state unnecessary?

The commentary's central claim is that communism removes the *class* basis of suppression, and with it the need for the state as a special machine of coercion:

> "Lastly, only communism makes the state absolutely unnecessary, for there is nobody to be suppressed--'nobody' in the sense of a class, of a systematic struggle against a definite section of the population." (State and Revolution · Chapter V: The Economic Basis of the Withering Away of the State)

It refuses to treat this as utopianism. The author concedes that individual "excesses" — violations of the rules of social intercourse — will still occur and still need stopping:

> "We are not utopians, and do not in the least deny the possibility and inevitability of excesses on the part of individual persons, or the need to stop such excesses." (State and Revolution · Chapter V)

But no special apparatus is required for that: "this will be done by the armed people themselves, as simply and as readily as any crowd of civilized people, even in modern society, interferes to put a stop to a scuffle or to prevent a woman from being assaulted" (State and Revolution · Chapter V).

The decisive argument is causal. The commentary locates the root of such excesses in material conditions — "the fundamental social cause of excesses... is the exploitation of the people, their want and their poverty" (State and Revolution · Chapter V). Remove that cause and the excesses themselves disappear: "With the removal of this chief cause, excesses will inevitably begin to 'wither away.' We do not know how quickly and in what succession, but we do know they will wither away. With their withering away the state will also wither away." (State and Revolution · Chapter V)

So the reasoning runs: no exploited class → no class to suppress → no special apparatus of suppression needed → individual disorder handled by the armed people themselves → and as the exploitation-caused excesses wither, the state withers with them. Note the deliberate agnosticism about timing and sequence — the outcome is asserted as certain, the schedule is not.

What does the commentary identify as the cause of grammar’s decline and the corruption of Arabic word meanings?

Two distinct causes are named, one for each decline.

**Grammar's decline:** Ibn Khaldūn ties it to the general decay of the sciences and crafts, which he in turn attributes to a decrease in civilization: "Grammar has come to the point of being allowed to disappear, along with the decrease in the other sciences and crafts which we have noted and which is the result of a decrease in civilization." (The Muqaddimah · The Various Kinds of Sciences)

**Corruption of Arabic word meanings:** the cause is sustained contact with non-Arabs, and the acceptance of their faulty Arabic. On lexicography the commentary says: "The habit of the Arabic language became corrupted. Rules for protecting the (vowel endings) were developed. However, the (process of) corruption continued on account of the close contact (of the Muslims) with non-Arabs. Eventually, it affected the conventional meanings of words. Many Arabic words were no longer used in their proper meaning. This was the result of indulgence shown to the incorrect language used by non-Arab speakers of Arabic in their terminologies, in contradiction to the pure Arabic language." (The Muqaddimah · The Various Kinds of Sciences)

So the two-part answer: grammar declines because civilization declines (with it, the sciences and crafts); word-meanings decay because of close contact with non-Arab speakers and tolerance of their incorrect usage. The stated remedy for the latter is to fix the conventional meanings in writing and systematic works, "because it was to be feared that they might be wiped out and that ignorance of the Qur'an and the traditions would result" (The Muqaddimah · The Various Kinds of Sciences) — the response that produced al-Khalīl b. Aḥmad's *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* and later works such as al-Jawharī's *Kitāb aṣ-Ṣiḥāḥ*.

According to this commentary, what must happen before the state disappears and true freedom becomes possible?

**Short answer: the state cannot disappear until classes and class resistance have disappeared** — that is, until no distinction remains between members of society in their relation to the means of production, and the capitalists' resistance has been broken.

The passage spells out the precondition directly:

> "Only in communist society, when the resistance of the capitalists have disappeared, when there are no classes (i.e., when there is no distinction between the members of society as regards their relation to the social means of production), only then 'the state... ceases to exist', and 'it becomes possible to speak of freedom'." (State and Revolution · Chapter V: The Economic Basis of the Withering Away of the State)

Two further points from the same commentary:

1. **Why it is gradual and spontaneous.** Lenin endorses the phrase "the state withers away" because it captures both features: "The expression 'the state withers away' is very well-chosen, for it indicates both the gradual and the spontaneous nature of the process." The mechanism is habit — people "will gradually become accustomed to observing the elementary rules of social intercourse" without force or coercion, once exploitation is gone.

2. **What comes first — the transitional phase.** Before full communism, there is the dictatorship of the proletariat, which "will for the first time create democracy for the people, for the majority, along with the necessary suppression of the exploiters, of the minority." Suppression is still necessary there, but it is now "the suppression of the exploiting minority by the exploited majority," and the special apparatus required is comparatively simple — "almost without a 'machine'... by the simple organization of the armed people."

So the sequence in this commentary is: capitalist state (dictatorship of the minority) → proletarian transitional state (democracy for the majority, suppression of the exploiters) → communism, where classes and class resistance are gone, democracy becomes complete, and only then does the state wither away "of its own accord."

How do varied work experiences and two kinds of knowledge compare as sources of insight?

The evidence points to two different models of insight: varied work experience appears as broad biographical preparation, while the “two seas” passage treats two kinds of knowledge as explicit, symbolic sources of spiritual insight.

For Frank Herbert, the varied work experience is listed as background, not directly interpreted as a theory of insight:

> “He worked a wide variety of jobs—including TV cameraman, radio commentator, oyster diver, jungle survival instructor, lay analyst, creative writing teacher, reporter and editor of several West Coast newspapers—before becoming a full-time writer.” (Chapterhouse Dune · About the Author)

That variety preceded his major literary emergence, but the evidence does not explain exactly how those jobs produced insight:

> “In 1952, Herbert began publishing science fiction with ‘Looking for Something?’ in Startling Stories. But his emergence as a writer of major stature did not occur until 1965, with the publication of Dune.” (Chapterhouse Dune · About the Author)

By contrast, the Study Quran passage explicitly interprets two kinds of knowledge as contrasting and complementary sources of insight:

> “The freshwater rivers, with their linear and directional nature, symbolize rational thought and knowledge of the Divine Law that leads to salvation or to God, while the saltwater sea, with its vastness, unpredictable currents, and fathomless depth, symbolizes deep inner knowledge and the infinite and all-encompassing nature of Divine Knowledge, or the Divine Itself, which human beings cannot ‘penetrate’ with linear or logical forms of knowing…” (The Study Quran · 18:60–61c · p. 1622)

It further identifies these as two “seas of knowledge”:

> “The two seas thus serve as a symbol of the different kinds of Divine Knowledge possessed by Moses and Khiḍr—Moses represents Divine Knowledge as manifested in Divine Law, and Khiḍr represents Divine Knowledge in direct and immediate form, the acquisition of which is the goal of the mystical path…” (The Study Quran · 18:60–61c · p. 1622)

So the comparison is this: the varied work experiences are presented as multiple worldly occupations preceding a writer’s major work, but the evidence does not spell out their causal role. The two kinds of knowledge, however, are expressly interpreted as distinct but related ways of knowing: one linear, rational, and law-oriented; the other vast, immediate, and mystical. In the evidence, the first is biographical context; the second is an explicit symbolic framework for insight.

What is the commentary saying about how Muad'Dib's mythos seeps into everyday life and religious devotion?

The commentary appears as an epigraph from the BOOK OF DIATRIBES (via the Hayt Chronicle), spoken in Muad'Dib's own voice — and it treats his mythos not as belief kept in temples but as a total environment absorbed into the most ordinary acts of living:

> "I've had a bellyful of the god and priest business! You think I don't see my own mythos? Consult your data once more, Hayt. I've insinuated my rites into the most elementary human acts. The people eat in the name of Muad'Dib! They make love in my name, are born in my name—cross the street in my name. A roof beam cannot be raised in the lowliest hovel of far Gangishree without invoking the blessing of Muad'Dib!" (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13)

So the seepage is described as saturation of the mundane: eating, sex, birth, walking, even carpentry — the raising of a roof beam — all become liturgical. Devotion is not an occasional observance but the medium of daily life, reaching "the lowliest hovel of far Gangishree," i.e., the periphery as much as the center.

The same chapter's dialogue frames that saturation critically. Edric argues the Atreides cultural program is a method of rule:

> "They dispense culture the better to rule. Beauty! They promote the beauty which enslaves. They create a literate ignorance—easiest thing of all. They leave nothing to chance. Chains! Everything they do forges chains, enslaves. But slaves always revolt." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13)

And Scytale's probe — "Never have philosophy and culture had such a patroness" (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13) — sets Alia up as the mythos's cultural patroness, while his closing observation, "It's this planet... It raises questions," and Edric's reply, "Planets don't speak!" / "This one does" (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13), tie the religion's momentum to Arrakis itself.

Context-based (outside the retrieved text): this is Herbert's familiar warning about messianic religion as an administered, self-perpetuating institution rather than private faith — the mythos becomes infrastructure, and Muad'Dib, seeing it clearly, is nevertheless trapped inside it. That reading is my own framing, not a library quotation.

Why do many who revolt against unjust rulers die unrewarded?

**Short answer:** Ibn Khaldūn's explanation is that such reformers perish unrewarded because they attempt a religious-political enterprise without the group feeling (*ʿaṣabiyya*) and the power needed to see it through — and God, in his account, commands such undertakings only where the power to succeed exists.

The central passage:

> "Many religious people who follow the ways of religion come to revolt against unjust amirs. They call for a change in, and prohibition of, evil practices. They hope for a divine reward for what they do. They gain many followers and sympathizers among the great mass of the people, but they risk being killed, and most of them actually do perish in consequence of their activities as sinners, unrewarded, because God had not destined them for such (activities). He commands such activities to be undertaken only where there exists the power to bring them to a successful conclusion." (The Muqaddimah · "On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks")

The reason is structural: dynasties are entrenched, and can be undermined "only through strong efforts backed by the group feeling of tribes and families." Even prophets, he notes, "depended on groups and families." Hence:

> "If someone who is on the right path were to attempt (religious reforms) in this way, his isolation would keep him from (gaining the support of) group feeling, and he would perish." (The Muqaddimah · "On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks")

And those who act from delusion rather than sincere devotion:

> "Many deluded individuals took it upon themselves to establish the truth. They did not know that they would need group feeling for that." (The Muqaddimah · "On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks")

He even illustrates it with al-ʿAbbās among the Ghumāra, who seized Bādīs and "was then killed, forty days after the start of his mission." His prescribed responses to such people: treat them as insane, punish them, or ridicule them as buffoons.

*Context (my own words, not a quotation):* this is Khaldūn's cyclical-sociology argument — moral rightness alone is insufficient; reform succeeds only when backed by the solidarity and coercive capacity to overturn an entrenched dynasty.

Why should God be remembered in a quiet voice rather than silently or aloud?

The reason is that the remembrance should be neither silent nor merely external/loud, but audible only to oneself so that body, soul, and spirit are all engaged together:

> “invocation or remembrance enjoined here should be done not silently, but in a voice low enough that it can be heard only by oneself, since there is a profound connection between the body, soul, and spirit—each of which is a door to the others—a connection that is activated by the process of remembering or invoking God. Hearing the invocation uttered by the bodily tongue moves the imagination and soul of the one invoking, which in turn strengthens the remembrance in the spiritual heart. The act of remembrance thus takes place simultaneously on all three levels, each reflecting upon and strengthening the others.” (The Study Quran · p. 1023)

The commentary also gives a historical reason for the quiet manner: the verse was revealed in Makkah, when believers had to worship circumspectly. It adds that Ibn ʿAjībah rejects using this verse to prohibit loud communal dhikr, noting that after the migration to Madinah the Prophet and Companions conducted public dhikr in the mosque (The Study Quran · p. 1023).

> “The well-known passage on the ‘withering away of the state’ in Anti-Dühring accuses the anarchists not simply of favoring the abolition of the state, but of preaching that the state can be abolished ‘overnight’.” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV)

Marx’s position, as quoted, was that the workers’ state is a **revolutionary and transient form**, kept to crush bourgeois resistance:

> “If the political struggle of the working class assumes revolutionary form … and if the workers set up their revolutionary dictatorship in place of the dictatorship of the bourgeoisie, they commit the terrible crime of violating principles, for in order to satisfy their wretched, vulgar everyday needs and to crush the resistance of the bourgeoisie, they give the state a revolutionary and transient form, instead of laying down their arms and abolishing the state.” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV)

Practically, the evidence stresses that even during the transition a certain form of state remains for ordinary social functions, but not a privileged bureaucratic apparatus:

> “The letting of houses owned by the whole people to individual families presupposes the collection of rent, a certain amount of control, and the employment of some standard in allotting the housing. All this calls for a certain form of state, but it does not at all call for a special military bureaucratic apparatus, with officials occupying especially privileged positions. The transition to a situation in which it will be possible to supply dwellings rent-free depends on the complete ‘withering away’ of the state.” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV)

Thus the evidence supports a gradualist account: the proletarian state is a transient instrument during the transition, and its full withering is tied to the abolition of classes and class resistance. But because the evidence gives no substantive theory or practice of **socialist democracy**, no grounded comparison between the two can be made from the provided texts.

How do debt bondage and delegation by verbal orders each create risks when people depend on someone else’s authority?

The evidence does not compare the two directly, but each passage shows a distinct risk arising from dependence on another’s authority.

Debt bondage creates risk because a debtor’s family members or dependents are placed under a creditor’s power, and that power can be abused. The text says creditors were “often mistreating the debt-pledges” and that “Physical abuse was common” (And Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 27). Even after repayment, the dependent could remain trapped:

> “Some creditors tried to hold onto pledges despite the fact that the debtor had paid off his obligation. No doubt some got away with this, particularly when debtors did not know their rights, lost their case as a result of judicial favoritism or outright bribery, or feared creditor retaliation if they protested.” (And Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 27)

So the pledged person depends on the creditor’s authority and is exposed to mistreatment, overlong bondage, and legal or retaliatory powerlessness.

Delegation by verbal orders creates risk because a ruler depends on subordinates to act wisely without written instructions, and those subordinates may hide problems or avoid decisions. Leto explains that such rulers are surrounded by people able to act on verbal orders, but:

> “Often, the most important piece of information is that something has gone wrong. Bad administrators hide their mistakes until it’s too late to make corrections.” (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28)

The danger is worsened because systems may select for the wrong kind of subordinate:

> “Most bureaucracies before mine sought out and promoted people who avoided decisions.” (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 28)

Thus dependence on delegated authority can mean errors are concealed and decisions are not made until too late.

Why might a servant choose to stay with his master instead of going free?

A bondservant might stay because the resources given at release were too meagre to build a better life, and because household slaves were often treated as family members:

> "One factor prompting this latter choice no doubt was the habit, common almost down to modern times, to treat house slaves as family members. The bondsman may have chosen to remain in the creditor's family when he realized what his master was giving him along with his freedom was not enough to make a better life." (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 35)

The choice is embedded in the Exodus law itself, which provides a ritual for it: if the servant declares "I love my master, my wife, and my children and do not want to go free," his master "shall take him to the door or the doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl. Then he will be his servant for life." (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 35)

Note the wider context in the same chapter: in Exodus 21 a freed bondservant was sent out "empty-handed," whereas the Deuteronomic Priestly Code required the former master to give him enough to be self-supporting. The choice to remain therefore reflects the economics of manumission — freedom without means could mean destitution and relapse into debt.

Gender mattered too: most female slaves and bondservants "were taken as concubines for the creditor or his sons, for whom they bore children," and Exodus did not call for their liberation, only humane treatment (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 35).

Beyond the library text: generally, ancient Near Eastern manumission could mean losing food, shelter, and kin ties within the household, so a servant with a wife and children acquired in the master's house — or one facing debt or famine outside — might rationally trade legal freedom for security.

How does self-consciousness compare with social consciousness in shaping human fulfillment and historical change?

Self-consciousness and social consciousness operate differently but complementarily. In the Hegel/Kojève evidence, self-consciousness is the decisive condition for human fulfillment and for completing historical change: “the perfect Man, the Man fully ‘satisfied’ by what he is, can only be a Man who knows what he is, who is fully self-conscious” (Kojeve · Chapter VII). Historical evolution reaches its end when action is conceptually grasped: “The phenomenon that completes the historical evolution and thus makes the absolute Science possible, therefore, is the ‘conception’ (Begreifen) of Napoleon by Hegel. This dyad, formed by Napoleon and Hegel, is the perfect Man, fully and definitively ‘satisfied’ by what he is and by what he knows himself to be” (Kojeve · Chapter VII).

Social consciousness, by contrast, carries the universal dimension of human existence—State, Society, People—but in religious form it lacks self-recognition. Religious man “substantializes and externalizes the concept (Begriff) of Spirit by re-presenting (Vorstellen) it to himself in the form of a Being (Sein) existing outside of Man... While in fact talking about himself, religious Man believes that he is talking about a God” (Kojeve · Chapter VII). Philosophy and theology “necessarily coexist: while opposing one another, they engender and mutually complete one another”: philosophy gives self-consciousness but isolates the particular individual, while theology “unawares, reveals the universal aspect of human existence: the State, Society, the People” (Kojeve · Chapter VII).

In the Stalin material, social consciousness is treated as conditioned by material life. Historical materialism addresses “the relation between social being and social consciousness, between the conditions of development of material life and the development of the spiritual life of society,” and it denies that geographical environment or population growth is the determining force of social development (Stalin · Dialectical and Historical Materialism). Thus self-consciousness appears as the completing, fulfilling moment of history, while social consciousness appears as the universal/social content—either unconscious in religion or materially determined in historical materialism.

What does the commentary suggest about the city woman's motive for killing the Priest?

The passage frames her motive as fear-driven silencing, not necessity: Jessica notes the woman had no practical reason to act, so the killing betrays panic.

> "The creature in the gaudy dress obviously had killed the Priest to make sure he was silenced." (Children of Dune · Chapter 23)

> "Why did she bother? Jessica wondered. She had only to wait for the man to die of asphyxiation. The act was a desperate one, a sign of deep fear." (Children of Dune · Chapter 23)

So the commentary offers two linked points: (1) the overt purpose was to guarantee the Priest could not talk — he had to be silenced; and (2) since asphyxiation would have killed him anyway, rushing to finish him off makes no sense except as an expression of "deep fear" — Jessica reads it as "a desperate one," a sign the conspiracy felt exposed.

The surrounding scene reinforces this reading: the woman wears "the gaudy garb of a city Fremen" yet performs "the ancient keening of her people," which Jessica registers as "the persistence of the old ways even as she saw the falseness in this city woman" (Children of Dune · Chapter 23). The dissonance between the ritual and the murder is what Jessica takes as evidence that the killing was a cover-up — the act of someone afraid of what the Priest might say, not a ritual necessity. Alia's own unconcern ("Have him removed," "Those who threaten me die") is read by Jessica as a sign that Alia "was a part of that conspiracy" (Children of Dune · Chapter 23).
