What did Moley and Tugwell consider the essence of the New Deal’s political philosophy?

Moley and Tugwell took the essence of the New Deal's political philosophy to be the subordination of creditor claims to the public interest — putting the nation's own domestic recovery ahead of the demands of private international bankers:

> "Roosevelt and his economic nationalists put the public sector's Interest first, that of private creditors last. To Moley and Rex Tugwell, two of the leading members of Roosevelt's Brains Trust, that was the essence of the New Deal's political philosophy." (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2: "Breakdown of World Balance, 1921–1932")

Two supporting threads in the same passage:

- **Domestic priority over internationalism.** "America's leaders thus looked first to the domestic economy" rather than to world financial readjustment, and Roosevelt, Moley and Tugwell "took a much less internationalist position" than Hoover's circle — whose sympathies, in Moley's account, leaned "heavily upon advice from New York, especially from the partners of the Morgan company" (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2).
- **Debt cancellation seen as creditor self-interest.** The Eastern bankers' support for cancelling or reducing the war debts was, on this reading, driven by the wish to revive "their own international loan business" — "That was the essence of their internationalist position" (Super Imperialism · Chapter 2).

**Library-based:** the identification above and the quoted lines. **Context-based note:** the surrounding OCR is partly scrambled, so some adjacent sentences (e.g. the fragment about Tugwell and "any relationship with the New York banking community") cannot be quoted reliably. **Own knowledge (not from the library):** this fits the wider Brains Trust idea of a "nationalist" New Deal that would rebuild the home economy first and treat foreign lending and war-debt collection as secondary — a stance Hudson sets against Hoover's and Stimson's internationalist, banker-aligned line.

How does eternity compare with time in shaping how we understand reality?

The evidence treats eternity as the nontemporal, permanent side of truth, while time is where truth actually appears and where finite existence plays out. In the Kojeve/Hegel passage, eternity is tied to truth’s unchangeable validity:

> “truth in the strict sense of the term is supposed to be a thing that cannot be either modified or denied: it is, as we say, ‘universally and necessarily’ valid—i.e., it is not subject to changes; it is, as we also say, eternal or nontemporal. On the other hand, there is no doubt that it is found at a certain moment of time and that it exists in time, because it exists through and for Man who lives in the World.” (Kojeve_IntroToHegel · Sixth Lecture)

So eternity gives reality its stable, universal character, while time is the medium through which that truth becomes present to human beings. Hegel then makes the relation even tighter:

> “Die Zeit ist der Begriff selbst, der da ist” (“Time is the Concept itself, which is there [in empirical existence]”). (Kojeve_IntroToHegel · Sixth Lecture)

In other words, time is not simply opposed to eternal truth; it is the Concept in its concrete, empirical existence.

The Dune passage gives a more existential comparison. There, eternity is what ultimately reclaims reality, while time is the instrument of finite, embodied life:

> “The flesh surrenders itself, he thought. Eternity takes back its own. Our bodies stirred these waters briefly, danced with a certain intoxication before the love of life and self, dealt with a few strange ideas, then submitted to the instruments of Time. What can we say of this? I occurred. I am not…” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 11)

Thus, across the evidence, eternity shapes understanding by supplying permanence, truth, or ultimate ownership, while time shapes understanding by making reality empirical, sequential, and finite.

How do debt-repayment pressures and contradictions in productive forces each push nations toward political conflict or upheaval?

Debt-repayment pressures push nations toward political conflict by turning creditor-debtor relations into trade retaliation, defaults, and allied disunity. Hudson records Britain’s warning “with the veiled threat that if war-debt payments were to be resumed the United Kingdom would have to strengthen its exchange position through measures further restricting British purchases of American goods” (Super Imperialism · Chapter 3). He compares this to “today’s Third World countries arguing that if America insists on payment of dollar loans, it must open its agricultural, textile and steel markets to debtor countries, and let these countries protect their markets from U.S. suppliers” (Super Imperialism · Chapter 3). The pressure also split the European allies: “Britain paid in full on December 15, but France defaulted,” and the French government fell, leading Hudson to write, “Another step was being taken on the path leading toward World War II” (Super Imperialism · Chapter 3).

Contradictions in productive forces push toward upheaval more structurally, by making existing relations of production obstacles to development. Stalin’s 1938 text states that when relations of production fail to correspond to the productive forces, “This results in economic crises, which lead to the destruction of productive forces. Furthermore, this incongruity itself constitutes the economic basis of social revolution, the purpose of which is to destroy the existing relations of production and to create new relations of production corresponding to the character of the productive forces” (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · 1938). Thus the productive forces are “not only the most mobile and revolutionary element in production, but are also the determining element in the development of production” (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · 1938).

What does the commentary say about efforts to boost domestic manufacturing after independence?

Aptheker's chapter on the economics of the Revolution stresses deliberate public promotion of domestic industry, both by the states and through the war itself.

State-level measures:
> "Thus, several States exempted from taxation for varying periods many different kinds of manufacturing; land was granted in other instances; bounties in still others; and loans, at very low interest rates, were also not uncommon. Meanwhile, through tariffs and other kinds of restrictive legislation, States further assisted capitalist enterprise." (Aptheker, American Revolution · The Economic Effects of the Revolution)

Wartime and post-war production, quoting Arthur H. Cole:
> "During the war 'there was an outburst of domestic production unlike anything that had gone before,'" (Aptheker, American Revolution · The Economic Effects of the Revolution)

with the result that "By 1790 Pennsylvania equalled Great Britain as the South's source of manufactured goods; by the same year the American demand for glass and paper was being met by American factories." (Aptheker, American Revolution · The Economic Effects of the Revolution)

Institutional and structural change followed: "A spurt in manufacturing, especially in textiles and metals appeared; a significant reduction in complete dependence upon British credit began; banks and other pooled commercial efforts started, through joint-stock methods, in turnpike, bridge and canal building, in manufacturing and in land speculation." (Aptheker, American Revolution · The Economic Effects of the Revolution)

Summary statistics from Robert A. East on chartering activity, which Aptheker quotes:
> "In contrast with the half dozen American business charters granted in the entire colonial period, eleven were issued in the United States between 1781 and 1785, twenty-two between 1786 and 1790, and one hundred and fourteen between 1791 and 1795." (Aptheker, American Revolution · The Economic Effects of the Revolution)

His overall verdict: the war and its aftermath, including the ending of British mercantile restrictions and the opening of new trade routes, "helped American capitalism emerge from infancy to childhood," and the economy of 1790 "was notably different from that of 1770." (Aptheker, American Revolution · The Economic Effects of the Revolution)

Note: this is a Marxist-framed economic history; the "commentary" here is Aptheker's own analysis plus the Cole and East material he cites.

> "When population increases, the available labour again increases. In turn, luxury again increases in correspondence with the increasing profit, and the customs and needs of luxury increase. The more numerous and the more abundant the population in a city, the more luxurious is the life of its inhabitants. This applies equally to all levels of the population." Who came to tell Abram that his nephew Lot had been taken captive along with his possessions?

A survivor (a fugitive from the battle) brought Abram the news.

> "A survivor came and brought the news to Abram the Hebrew, * who was camping at the oak of Mamre the Amorite, a kinsman of Eshcol and Aner; these were allies of Abram." (The Catholic Study Bible, New American Bible Revised Edition · Book 106, ch107)

The passage goes on to describe Abram's response: "When Abram heard that his kinsman had been captured, he mustered three hundred and eighteen of his retainers, born in his house, and went in pursuit as far as Dan" — and he recovered both Lot and his possessions (The Catholic Study Bible · Book 106, ch107). Note that the biblical text does not name the survivor; the source materials in this library give no personal name for him, so any identification by name would come from later tradition or commentary rather than from the passage itself.

How do hidden inner meanings compare with answers that seem sensible but explain nothing?

The evidence never places these two ideas side by side, so the comparison itself is mine, not the library's. But the library does supply a sharp statement of one side and a body of material for the other.

**The warning against sensible-sounding answers** is the epigraph to a Dune chapter:

> "Answers are a perilous grip on the universe. They can appear sensible yet explain nothing." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 41)

The surrounding scene reinforces it — Odrade weaponizes surface chatter against watchers ("Concealing and secret. Words to annoy the watchers.") (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 41), deliberately using plausible, empty talk as camouflage.

**Hidden inner meanings**, by contrast, appear in the Study Quran's apparatus as a recognized interpretive tradition, not a defect. The footnotes point to a ḥadīth on the levels of interior meaning and their mapping onto seven subtle centers:

> "On al-Simnānī's coordination of the levels of interior meaning mentioned in this ḥadīth with the seven subtle centers, see Sands, Ṣūfī Commentaries, 44." (The Study Quran · p. 4065)

Further references include al-Shahrastānī's esoteric commentary, *Mafātīḥ al-asrār* (The Study Quran · p. 4068), and the author's own study of it, "For an analysis of his system and its application to Sūrah 1, al-Fātiḥah, see my *Keys to the Arcana: Shahrastānī's Esoteric Commentary on the Qur'an*" (The Study Quran · p. 4070). The same apparatus cites al-Ghazzālī's *Jawāhir al-Qurʾān*, translated as *The Jewels of the Qur'an* (The Study Quran · p. 4073), and al-Suyūṭī on "knowledge" meaning "principles of knowledge" (The Study Quran · p. 4075).

So, in my own words: a hidden inner meaning is a claimed layer *beneath* a text that the interpreter must reach; the Zensunni warning targets an answer that *stops* at the surface and mistakes its tidiness for truth. One is depth-seeking; the other is a caution that depth may be absent even when the surface satisfies. The two are complementary rather than contrary — the epigraph supplies the reason one would pursue inner meanings at all, since a merely sensible answer can be "a perilous grip on the universe" (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 41).

**Short answer:** From the evidence, only grammar is directly documented. Ibn Khaldūn treats grammar/lexicography as a *preservative* discipline — rules are written down because the living habit of the language is decaying, and learners are given "elementary rules for beginners" before the science itself withers. How do commercial freedom and class conflict each explain the causes and aims of revolutions?

The evidence presents two related but distinct explanations:

**Commercial freedom** views revolution as an effort to escape imperial trade restrictions and win economic self-government. In Aptheker’s survey, Emory R. Johnson states:

> “The Revolution in America was fought to secure commercial and industrial freedom through the establishment of political liberty. ... The Revolutionary War was fought to secure freedom of trade and to obtain home rule in the levying of taxes for the support of the government.” (Aptheker American Revolution · The Nature of the Revolution)

J. Franklin Jameson similarly stresses trade restrictions:

> “... of the deep underlying causes, which for a generation had been moving the American in the direction of independence, none was so potent, according to all the best testimony, as the parliamentary restrictions on the trade of the colonies.” (Aptheker American Revolution · The Nature of the Revolution)

Edward Channing makes the aim explicit:

> “Commercialism, the desire for advantage and profit in trade and industry, was at the bottom of the struggle between England and America...” (Aptheker American Revolution · The Nature of the Revolution)

So in this account, the cause is mercantile restriction, and the aim is commercial freedom plus home rule over taxation and trade.

**Class conflict** explains revolution as the product of irreconcilable economic class antagonisms. Aptheker notes that the Beard–Hacker version emphasized:

> “... its use of words like bourgeoisie and its concentration upon conflicting needs of British mercantilism and rising American capitalism...” (Aptheker American Revolution · The Nature of the Revolution)

More broadly, the Marxist analysis in *State and Revolution* treats the state itself as arising from class conflict:

> “Rather, it is a product of society at a certain stage of development; it is the admission that this society has become entangled in an insoluble contradiction with itself, that it has split into irreconcilable antagonisms which it is powerless to dispel. But in order that these antagonisms, these classes with conflicting economic interests, might not consume themselves and society in fruitless struggle, it became necessary to have a power, seemingly standing above society...” (State and Revolution · Chapter I)

Thus, in the class-conflict account, revolutions are not merely about trade policy or taxation but about class power, rooted in the struggle of:

> “... revolutionary thinkers and leaders of oppressed classes fighting for emancipation.” (State and Revolution · Chapter I)

What does the commentary say about Hegel’s claim that the Battle of Jena marks history’s completion through the master-slave dialectic?

Kojève’s commentary presents Hegel’s claim as central to his absolute knowledge: the Napoleonic Wars, especially the Battle of Jena, complete History by dialectically overcoming both Master and Slave.

> “Now, according to Hegel, it is in and by the wars of Napoleon, and, in particular, the Battle of Jena, that this completion of History is realized through the dialectical overcoming (Aufheben) of both the Master and the Slave. Consequently, the presence of the Battle of Jena in Hegel's consciousness is of capital importance. It is because Hegel hears the sounds of that battle that he can know that History is being completed or has been completed, that consequently—his conception of the World is a total conception, that his knowledge is an absolute knowledge.” (Kojeve_IntroToHegel · p. 46)

The commentary also says this completion is tied to the synthesis of Mastery and Slavery:

> “History will be completed at the moment when the synthesis of the Master and the Slave is realized, that synthesis that is the whole Man, the Citizen of the universal and homogeneous State created by Napoleon.” (Kojeve_IntroToHegel · p. 46)

So, in Kojève’s reading, Hegel treats the Battle of Jena as the historical event through which the master-slave dialectic reaches its resolution, producing the completed universal state and making Hegel’s own philosophy possible as absolute knowledge.

What does it mean that the prophet’s mission is first to uproot and tear down, and only then to build and plant?

The order is deliberate and programmatic: demolition comes first because Judah must be cleared of what is false before anything true can be planted, and the same three-part language frames the whole book.

The study note states the commission outright:

> "Jeremiah's commission is dual: with the words God places in his mouth he is both 'to uproot and tear down, to destroy and to demolish' and 'to build and to plant' (Jer 1:10). The negative aspect of the prophetic mission is given double play here, suggesting the dominant tone of the prophetic oracles and narratives that follow." (The Catholic Study Bible NABRE · Book 52, ch. 53)

Yet the sequence is not two unrelated vocations — the note stresses it is one process with an order:

> "Yet destructive activity is the first part of a sequence that includes constructive activity, implying a larger process in which replanting follows preparing the field (cf. Is 28:23–29)." (The Catholic Study Bible NABRE · Book 52, ch. 53)

So the tearing down is preparatory, like clearing and breaking ground: it is not the goal, but nothing can be built until it happens. The note also observes that this language recurs throughout Jeremiah and functions as an epitome of the book's message:

> "The language of this commission recurs throughout the book of Jeremiah, appearing three times in the first part (Jer 1:10; 18:7–9; 24:6) and three times in the second (Jer 31:28; 42:10; 45:4). It serves as a summary of the overall outlook of the book: ruin and desolation in the present but the possibility of a new start in the more distant future." What makes him feel like a monster and a freak?

Paul feels like a monster and a freak because he can trace, with terrible clarity, exactly how he was made — and the making was not his own.

He sees the causal chain in his own past:

> "He could look to his own past and see the start of it—the training, the sharpening of talents, the refined pressures of sophisticated disciplines, even exposure to the O.C. Bible at a critical moment…and, lastly, the heavy intake of spice." (Dune · Chapter 22)

Every link is deliberate: Bene Gesserit conditioning, the "refined pressures," and then the spice of Arrakis itself. The result is his outburst:

> "I'm a monster! he thought. A freak!" (Dune · Chapter 22)

The monster is not a moral confession but the recognition of being a manufactured thing — the fulfillment of someone else's project. When his mother reaches for him, he accuses her directly:

> "You didn't want a son!" he said. "You wanted a Kwisatz Haderach! You wanted a male Bene Gesserit!" (Dune · Chapter 22)

and

> "But not the training," he said. "Not the things that…awakened…the sleeper." (Dune · Chapter 22)

What makes it unbearable rather than merely unsettling is that the awakening cannot be shut off. He names the spice as the trigger and himself as the special case:

> "It's the spice," he said. "It's in everything here—the air, the soil, the food, the geriatric spice. It's like the Truthsayer drug. It's a poison!" (Dune · Chapter 22)

> "A poison—so subtle, so insidious…so irreversible. It won't even kill you unless you stop taking it. We can't leave Arrakis unless we take part of Arrakis with us." (Dune · Chapter 22)

> "You and the spice," Paul said. "The spice changes anyone who gets this much of it, but thanks to you , I could bring the change to consciousness. I don't get to leave it in the unconscious where its disturbance can be blanked out. I can see it." (Dune · Chapter 22)

So the freakishness is twofold: he is the inherited product of a breeding and training programme he never consented to, and the spice has made his own transformation visible to him — he "can see it" in the new way, an implacable part of him recording his own breakdown as "an interesting emotional datum." He is trapped in Arrakis, and trapped in a self he did not choose.

What does the commentary say about Zion’s role in celebrating God’s victory?

The commentary presents Zion as the fitting—indeed the appointed—place to celebrate the victory God won for Israel:

> "Psalm 76 A song glorifying Zion, the mountain of Jerusalem where God destroyed Israel's enemies. Zion is thus the appropriate site to celebrate the victory (Ps 76:3–4), a victory described in parallel scenes (Ps 76:5–7, 8–11). Israel is invited to worship its powerful patron deity (Ps 76:12)." (The Catholic Study Bible · Book 133)

Supporting notes on the same psalm sharpen the picture of Zion's role:

- The name "Salem" ties the site to Jerusalem and, by wordplay, to peace: "76:3 Salem: an ancient name for Jerusalem, used here perhaps on account of its allusion to the Hebrew word for peace, shalom, cf. Gn 14:18; Heb 7:1–3." (The Catholic Study Bible · Book 133)
- The mountains of Zion are cosmically significant, not merely local: "76:5 Ancient mountains: conjectural translation of a difficult Hebrew phrase on the basis of Gn 49:26. The mountains are part of the structure of the universe (Ps 89:12–13)." (The Catholic Study Bible · Book 133)

So the structure the commentary gives is: God defeats Israel's enemies *at* Zion (the mountain of Jerusalem), and therefore Zion is the appropriate place for the community to celebrate that victory and to worship its "powerful patron deity" (Ps 76:12). The celebration is not incidental to the location—the site of the victory is the site of the liturgy.

A related thread in the next psalm's notes gives Zion a second, larger role in God's mercy: "78:68, 70 God's ultimate offer of mercy to the sinful, helpless people is Zion and the Davidic king." (The Catholic Study Bible · Book 133) Nothing in the retrieved evidence goes beyond these notes; any fuller theology of Zion as the locus of victory-celebration would be my own contextualizing, not library text.

How do superstition and political bargaining shape what people will sacrifice—lives or settlements?

Superstition tends to sacrifice settlements and infrastructure, while political bargaining tends to treat people—especially family members—as currency to be spent.

Political bargaining frames lives and succession as negotiable prices. The Reverend Mother opens by asking what Paul will pay for Chani:

> “much was he really prepared to pay for his Chani’s life? Would he accept a cross with his own sister?” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 12)

Irulan is explicitly reduced to a spendable asset:

> “Wasn’t she trained to be used?” Paul asked. (Dune Messiah · Chapter 12)

> “Well . . . Irulan’s a divided coin. Was there another way to spend such a coin?” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 12)

Even the throne and the next generation become bargaining chips:

> “Will you put Chani’s child on the throne?” the Reverend Mother asked.  
> “On my throne,” Paul said. (Dune Messiah · Chapter 12)

Superstition, by contrast, drives the Fremen to abandon settlements. The text says:

> “Superstitious fear ruled the new Fremen” (Children of Dune · Chapter 58)

One settlement is surrendered after repeated losses:

> “This djedida had been given back to the desert after its qanat had been shattered a fifth time in eleven months. Four times they’d repaired the ravages of the Desert Demon, then they’d no longer had the surplus water to risk another loss.” (Children of Dune · Chapter 58)

The result is widespread abandonment:

> “Eight out of nine new settlements had been abandoned.” (Children of Dune · Chapter 58)

The Fremen read natural events as divine judgments:

> “They saw omens in everything. Were worms increasingly scarce except in the Tanzerouft? It was the judgment of Shai-Hulud!” (Children of Dune · Chapter 58)

Superstition also intersects with political reaction: many Fremen believe the Desert Demon is a revolutionary force that would overthrow Alia and restore older ways (Children of Dune · Chapter 58). Ghanima even contemplates sacrificing lives in that conflict:

> “I’d join you myself, but I’ve a knife yet unblooded. Alia and Farad’n. Farad’n and Alia. The Old Baron’s her demon, and that can’t be permitted.” (Children of Dune · Chapter 58)

So in these passages, political bargaining sacrifices persons, heirs, and loyalties, while superstition sacrifices settlements and the material world of the djedidas, with both forces capable of turning toward the sacrifice of lives.

When economic collapse destroys livelihoods, does it push people toward revolution or toward stubborn endurance?

The strongest economic-structural answer in the evidence is that economic crisis pushes toward **revolution**, not mere endurance.

> “This results in economic crises, which lead to the destruction of productive forces. Furthermore, this incongruity itself constitutes the economic basis of social revolution, the purpose of which IS to destroy the existing relations of production and to create new relations of production corresponding to the character of the productive forces.”  
> (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · p. 22)

The same source contrasts that with socialism, where the relations of production correspond to the productive forces and therefore “economic crises and the destruction of productive forces are unknown” (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · p. 22).

A separate passage does offer a motto of stubborn endurance, though it is not specifically about economic collapse:

> “Remember! We are the ancient doll: seven times down, eight times up.”  
> (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 12)

So the evidence gives no single universal answer: the economic text treats crisis as the basis for social revolution, while the Dune passage expresses endurance as a cultural ethos in a different context.

What does this commentary say about whether remembering God quietly forbids loud communal dhikr?

**No — the commentary presents quiet remembrance as the general injunction, but explicitly rejects the inference that this forbids loud communal *dhikr*.**

The passage first explains why remembrance is to be voiced quietly rather than silently:

> "invocation or remembrance enjoined here should be done not silently, but in a voice low enough that it can be heard only by oneself, since there is a profound connection between the body, soul, and spirit—each of which is a door to the others—a connection that is activated by the process of remembering or invoking God." (The Study Quran · p. 1023)

It then names and answers the objection directly:

> "Because of the injunction to remember God quietly, some might consider this verse as prohibiting the loud, communal dhikr practiced by Sufi groups. Ibn ʿAjībah, however, rejects this interpretation, noting that this verse was revealed in Makkah, when the believers had to be circumspect in their worship, and that when the community migrated to Madinah, the Prophet and Companions would conduct public dhikr sessions in the mosque." (The Study Quran · p. 1023)

So the commentary's position is: the quiet-voice injunction reflects the Makkan circumstances of concealment, not a blanket ban on public *dhikr*. Ibn ʿAjībah's counter-evidence is the Prophet's and Companions' public *dhikr* sessions in the Madinan mosque. The same section adds that morning and evening are singled out as times suited to remembrance, and may also signify that one should remember and praise God at all times (The Study Quran · p. 1023).

Context note (not from the library text): the verse in question is understood to be Q 7:205, and the debate over silent vs. vocal *dhikr* is a long-standing one among jurists and Sufi commentators — the library evidence above reflects the Sufi-leaning side of that debate.

How does the pursuit of economic stability compare with the lure of spiritual desire?

The evidence does not directly compare the two, but the passages point to a contrast.

In the economic material, stability is an external, systemic goal. It turns on liquidity, credit, and trade:

> “Foreigners could not buy American exports without a means of payment, and private creditors were not eager to extend further loans to countries that were not creditworthy.” (Super Imperialism · Introduction)

The logic is counterintuitive but aimed at balance:

In the *Dune* passage, spiritual desire is not a balance to be managed but an internal, incurable burning. The Wormsong asks:

> “Oh, worm of many teeth,

Here desire is consuming, mystical, and beyond remedy: it has “no cure,” and there is no “robe” to cover its “burnings.”

So, within the evidence, the pursuit of economic stability appears as a collective, rational, external balancing act; the lure of spiritual desire appears as a personal, overwhelming, inward fire. One seeks equilibrium through institutions and payments, the other describes surrender to a longing that cannot be cured or hidden.

Why are Christians described as nearest in affection to those who believe?

**Short answer:** The Quran grounds it in two things — the presence of priests and monks among them, and their lack of arrogance — and the Study Quran's commentary adds that Christians' "nearness in affection" made it comparatively easier for them to accept the Quranic message, and that certain Christians played pivotal supportive roles in the Prophet's life.

The verse itself:

> "And thou wilt find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say, 'We are Christians.' That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant." (The Study Quran · 5:82, p. 703)

And its continuation, describing their response to revelation:

> "And when they hear that which was sent down unto the Messenger, thou seest their eyes overflow with tears because of the truth they recognize. They say, 'Our Lord, we believe, so inscribe us among the witnesses.'" (The Study Quran · 5:83, p. 703)

The commentary explains: "in v. 82 Jews and Christians are differentiated with regard to their attitude toward Muslim believers. Here the Jews are described as the most hostile to the believers, along with the idolaters … while the Christians are said to be the nearest … in affection to Muslim believers" (The Study Quran · Sūrah 5 commentary, p. 703). It adds that "the Christians' 'nearness in affection' to the believers made it comparatively easier for them to accept the Quranic message," and that "In v. 82, the Christians' nearness to the Muslim believers is attributed partly to the presence of priests and monks" (The Study Quran · Sūrah 5 commentary, p. 703–704).

The commentary also gives the historical grounding: "It thus seems more plausible to contextualize this verse within the life of the Prophet and the early Muslim community," noting that "certain Christian figures played positive and pivotal roles in the Prophet's early life and mission" — the monk Baḥīrah, Waraqah (Khadījah's cousin), and the Negus of Abyssinia who sheltered Makkan Muslims (The Study Quran · Sūrah 5 commentary, p. 703–704). It cautions that some read the verse as absolute, an interpretation "belied by the fact that at various points in Islamic history Muslims had better relations with the Jews than with Christians" (p. 703), and notes that it praises Christians generally, not only those who converted (p. 704).

What does the commentary say about Engels’s view of the state in his letter to Bebel?

The commentary treats Engels’s letter to Bebel as a major statement on the state. It calls the letter’s observation “one of the most, if not the most, remarkable observation on the state in the works of Marx and Engels” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV).

In that letter, Engels criticizes the Gotha Programme’s talk of a “free people’s state” and a “free state”:

> “The whole talk about the state should be dropped, especially since the Commune, which was no longer a state in the proper sense of the word.” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV)

Engels’s central point, as the commentary presents it, is that the state is a temporary instrument of class coercion, not a vehicle of freedom:

> “As the state is only a transitional institution which is used in the struggle, in the revolution, to hold down one's adversaries by force, it is sheer nonsense to talk of a 'free people's state'; so long as the proletariat still needs the state, it does not need it in the interests of freedom but in order to hold down its adversaries, and as soon as it becomes possible to speak of freedom the state as such ceases to exist.” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV)

The commentary also stresses that Engels proposed replacing “state” with “community,” using the German word *Gemeinwesen* or the French word *commune*. It argues that because Engels was living with Marx and the letter concerned the same programme Marx criticized weeks later, Engels’s “we” included Marx:

> “Consequently, when he says “we” in the last sentence, Engels undoubtedly, in his own as well as in Marx's name, suggests to the leader of the German workers' party that the word “state” be struck out of the programme and replaced by the word “community.”” (State and Revolution · Chapter IV)

The commentary adds that “present-day ‘Marxism,’ which has been falsified for the convenience of the opportunists,” would howl “anarchism” at such an amendment, but the Bolsheviks should follow Engels’s and Marx’s advice in revising the party programme (State and Revolution · Chapter IV).

> 3.4 Mao Zedong 71 struggle, ‘socialist society grows more united and consolidated through the ceaseless process of correctly handling and resolving contradictions’ (Mao 1957a, 213; 1957b, 393). 3.4.2 Principal and Secondary Contradictions In regard to principal and secondary contradictions and their aspects, Mao devotes a significant annotation to the topic, going well beyond his source text (Mao 1988, 87-90; 1937k, 273-275). That text speaks only of the relation between a dominant aspect of a contradiction and its secondary aspect (see more below). By contrast, Mao immediately makes the distinction between principal and secondary contradictions, and then observes: “Because the development of the principal contradiction determines the development of the various secondary contradictions, if one cannot distinguish between the principal and secondary contradictions, between the determining contradiction and those that are determined, one cannot seek out the most essential thing of a process’ (Mao 1988, 87; 1937k, 273). As Knight suggests (2005, 156), there is a direct path from this annotation to the lectures and then the essay ‘On Contradiction’, so much so that we can see the structure of the later work already emerging as Mao was studying the Soviet sources. Even more, the need to identify the principal contradiction, as formulated by Mao, has come to guide CPC policy and the development of the New China until today; indeed, the determining feature of all government policy turns on identifying the principal contradiction to which all the other secondary contradictions relate. What does the commentary claim about Muslim control of the sea and their raids against Christian territories?

The commentary claims that, during the period of Fatimid and Kalbite strength, Muslims achieved naval dominance over the Mediterranean and used it to raid Christian territories:

> “During all that time, the Muslims were gaining control over the largest part of the high sea. Their fleets kept coming and going, and the Muslim armies crossed the sea in ships from Sicily to the great mainland opposite Sicily, on the northern shore. They fell upon the European Christian rulers and made massacres in their realms.” (The Muqaddimah · Chapter “On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks”)

It also describes Muslim fleets raiding specific Christian targets:

> “Mujahid al-‘Amiri, the master of Denia, one of the reyes de taifas, conquered the island of Sardinia with his fleet in the year 405 [1014/15].” (The Muqaddimah · Chapter “On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks”)

The commentary further claims that Christian fleets were forced to withdraw to the northeastern Mediterranean and that Muslim control became overwhelming:

> “The Christian nations withdrew with their fleets to the north-eastern side of the Mediterranean, to the coastal regions inhabited by the European Christians and the Slavs, and to the Aegean islands, and did not go beyond them. The Muslim fleet had pounced upon them as eagerly as lions upon their prey. They covered most of the surface of the Mediterranean with their equipment and numbers and travelled its lanes (on missions both) peaceful and warlike. Not a single Christian board floated on it.” (The Muqaddimah · Chapter “On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks”)

The same passage later notes that this dominance reversed after the Fatimid and Umayyad dynasties weakened, when Christians took control of islands and Syrian ports, but the core claim is that Muslim sea power and raids against Christian lands were extensive and dominant in that earlier period.

What does the commentary say about physical constants marking where gradual quantitative changes produce qualitative shifts?

The passage in question is Stalin's exposition — quoting Engels — of the dialectical law of the transformation of quantity into quality. The relevant answer is the "constants of physics" gloss:

> "What are known as the constants of physics (the point at which one state passes into another – J. St.) are in most cases nothing but designations for the nodal points at which a quantitative (change) increase or decrease of movement causes a qualitative change in the state of the given body, and at which, consequently, quantity is transformed into quality." (Revolution › Stalin · Dialectical and Historical Materialism)

Note the parenthetical "(the point at which one state passes into another – J. St.)" — the author/editor glossing the term for the reader. The preceding examples set this up: "A definite minimum current is required to make a platinum wire glow; every metal has its melting temperature; every liquid has a definite freezing point and boiling point at a given pressure... every gas has its critical point at which, by proper pressure and cooling, it can be converted into a liquid state" (Revolution › Stalin · Dialectical and Historical Materialism).

The commentary then extends it to chemistry:

> "Chemistry may be called the science of the qualitative changes which take place in bodies as the effect of changes of quantitative composition." (Revolution › Stalin · Dialectical and Historical Materialism)

with ozone (three oxygen atoms rather than two) and the different combining proportions of oxygen with nitrogen or sulphur as instances.

Finally, Engels' summary image, cited here as the "Hegelian nodal line of measure relations":

> "This is precisely the Hegelian nodal line of measure relations in which at certain definite nodal points, the purely quantitative increase or decrease gives rise to a qualitative leap, for example, in the case of water which is heated or cooled, where boiling point and freezing point are the nodes at which – under normal pressure – the leap to a new aggregate state takes place, and where consequently quantity is transformed into quality." (Revolution › Stalin · Dialectical and Historical Materialism)

So the claim is that physical constants are not mere numbers but *nodal points*: thresholds where continuous quantitative variation (heating, cooling, increasing current) abruptly yields a new qualitative state. The section immediately following ("d) Contradictions Inherent in Nature") carries the same idea forward, describing development as the "struggle" of opposites rather than harmonious unfolding.

Context note (not from the library): this is Stalin's 1938 summary of Engels' *Anti-Dühring* and *Dialectics of Nature*; the underlying Hegelian term is *Knotenlinie von Maßverhältnissen*, the nodal line of measure relations. Section numbering in the source is only partially visible in the retrieved excerpt, so the citation above is given by work rather than by a numbered section.

The text states:

> “Hence, the party of the proletariat should not guide itself in its practical activity by casual motives, but by the laws of development of society, and by practical deductions from these laws.” (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · Page 13)

So the argument is that society is not governed merely by “reason,” “universal morals,” or chance motives; it is governed by objective developmental laws that can be studied scientifically.

How does choosing qualified religious leaders compare with a leader’s myth becoming woven into everyday life?

**Short answer:** they are mirror-image strategies for the same problem — keeping the sacred from misleading people — but Ibn Khaldūn works by *exclusion at the gate*, while Herbert's Muad'Dib myth works by *saturation with no gate at all*.

**Khaldūn: qualification as a filter.** The ruler's duty is active vetting and exclusion:

> "caliph must examine the religious scholars and teachers and entrust it only to those who are qualified for it. He must help them in their task, and he must prevent those who are not qualified for the office from attaining it." (The Muqaddimah · On Dynasties, Royal Authority, Government Ranks)

The stated danger is pedagogical: the caliph "has to take care, lest unqualified persons undertake to act as mufti and so lead the people astray." (The Muqaddimah · same chapter) Note the second safeguard is internal, not institutional — teachers and muftis "must have some restraining influence in themselves that tells them not to undertake something for which they are not qualified, so that they may not lead astray those who ask for the right way or cause to stumble those who want to be guided." (same) So Khaldūn assumes religious authority *can* be rationed, and that correct transmission depends on competence plus conscience.

**Herbert: the myth has already bypassed qualification.** In Dune Messiah the ruler's mythos is no longer taught by credentialed teachers; it has colonized ordinary action:

> "The people eat in the name of Muad'Dib! They make love in my name, are born in my name—cross the street in my name. A roof beam cannot be raised in the lowliest hovel of far Gangishree without invoking the blessing of Muad'Dib!" (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13)

Where Khaldūn worries about the unqualified *teacher*, Herbert's Edric names the finished product — a culture that bypasses judgment altogether: "They dispense culture the better to rule. Beauty! They promote the beauty which enslaves. They create a literate ignorance—easiest thing of all. They leave nothing to chance. Chains! Everything they do forges chains, enslaves." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13) Scytale adds that the planet itself "raises questions" and "speaks of creation" (same), i.e. the myth is now environmental rather than curricular.

**The contrast:** Khaldūn's remedy is a gate — examine, entrust, prevent. Herbert's scenario is what happens when the gate is irrelevant because the myth is already in the bread, the marriage bed, and the roof beam. Both texts, however, share one premise: unvetted sacred authority leads people astray — Khaldūn fears the straying, Herbert depicts it as accomplished and industrial.

How do Lenin’s non-antagonistic contradictions compare with Marx’s unavoidable defects in communism’s first phase?

The evidence does not offer a direct side-by-side comparison, but it shows two related ways of thinking about what persists after capitalism is overthrown.

Lenin’s formulation treats remaining tensions as **non-antagonistic contradictions**. The discussion of his texts says that “those contradictions are not, as a rule, antagonistic” (Socialism With Chinese Characteristics · Chapter 74). It connects this to a dialectical materialist emphasis on “self-movement, on internal dynamics,” from which one then understands external forces (Socialism With Chinese Characteristics · Chapter 74). In other words, these are contradictions still at work inside the developing society, but they are not necessarily class-enemy oppositions requiring destructive suppression.

Marx’s “defect” in communism’s first phase is more concrete: the persistence of “bourgeois law” and therefore of actual inequality in distribution. Lenin’s text reports Marx as saying:

> “This is a ‘defect’, says Marx, but it is unavoidable in the first phase of communism; for if we are not to indulge in utopianism, we must not think that having overthrown capitalism people will at once learn to work for society without any rules of law.” (State and Revolution · Chapter V)

For that reason, even after the expropriation of the capitalists, a state remains necessary:

> “The state withers away insofar as there are no longer any capitalists, any classes, and, consequently, no class can be suppressed. But the state has not yet completely withered away, since the [there] still remains the safeguarding of ‘bourgeois law’, which sanctifies actual inequality.” (State and Revolution · Chapter V)

Thus the two ideas are compatible. Lenin supplies a broad dialectical category—non-antagonistic contradiction—for the tensions that continue within socialism, while Marx identifies one unavoidable concrete defect, the lingering reign of bourgeois law and inequality, which explains why the state and legal regulation cannot disappear until the higher phase of communism. Both reject the utopian expectation that overthrowing capitalism immediately creates a finished, fully equal society.

The comparison is the Quran's counter-argument to the inference that Jesus's fatherless birth makes him divine: Adam was created with neither father nor mother, yet no one calls him God's son — so the miracle of Jesus's birth proves God's creative power, not Jesus's divinity.

The verse itself:

The commentary supplies the context and the logic of the argument:

> "It is reported that these verses were revealed while the Christian delegation from Najrān was in Madinah... These Christians reportedly argued that since Jesus had no human father, he was truly God's son. This verse constitutes one of the central arguments in the Quran against the divinity of Christ. It acknowledges the miraculous nature of his birth, but rejects the implication that this makes him Divine. If God could create Adam, who had neither earthly father nor mother, from dust, he could also create Jesus from the 'blood' of Mary (R). The word likeness means that certain attributes of Adam and Jesus are alike (R)." (The Study Quran · 3:59)

The following verse reinforces the point — "The truth is from thy Lord; so be not among the doubters" — which the commentary glosses as an instruction "not to doubt the description of Jesus in the previous verse" (The Study Quran · 3:60).

Context (not quoted from the library): this is the *a fortiori* or *qiyās* argument — if a fatherless creation implies divinity, Adam, who had no parents at all, would have a stronger claim; since that conclusion is rejected, the premise fails.

How does the commentary explain the New Year's connection to restoring social balance and settling debts?

The passage explains the New Year as a recurring moment of renewal whose purpose was not only natural but social — a reset of balance, equity, and above all economic relations:

> "the start of a new period, above all the inauguration of a king's new reign. The idea was to renew not only nature but also social balance in general. The common denominator is to restore amity and equity in a celebratory setting. Many societies have released lawbreakers on such occasions. Three points stand out in this commentary:

1. **The occasion is tied to political renewal** — the paradigmatic New Year is "the inauguration of a king's new reign," so the ritual reset is bound up with a fresh start in authority and time.
2. **Renewal is double** — nature *and* "social balance in general"; the cosmic and the social are renewed together, not separately.
3. **The unifying purpose is amity and equity** — "The common denominator is to restore amity and equity in a celebratory setting." Debt settlement is presented as one instance of this broader restorative impulse, alongside the release of lawbreakers.

The passage also shows the practice is cross-cultural and ancient, not narrowly Near Eastern or biblical: Europeans, Asians, Africans, and Native Americans all use the New Year to clean house, gather kin, and "put their economic relations in order, especially by settling debts."

How does centralized state authority compare with the eventual loss of public power’s political character?

The evidence presents a contrast rather than a similarity. Centralized state authority appears as a top-down, coercive power that subordinates outlying communities. Aptheker describes England’s posture as:

> “England's determination to centralize authority at Whitehall and Westminster; to maintain her colonies in a permanent state ot subordination, politically as well as commercially; to deny them the status of self-governing communities” (Aptheker American Revolution · p. 17).

By contrast, the eventual loss of public power’s “political character” means the state ceases to function as an instrument of class coercion. The evidence explains:

> “for both Engels and Marx, ‘political character’ means the reality of class struggle and its manifestation in the state” (Socialism_With_Chinese_Characteristics · Chapter 245).

Therefore,

> “if public Gewalt loses its political character, it ceases to be a manifestation of class struggle and instrument of coercion” (Socialism_With_Chinese_Characteristics · Chapter 245).

This also affects ordinary political institutions: elections themselves “would cease to be politicised” (Socialism_With_Chinese_Characteristics · Chapter 245). Instead of a separated authority ruling over society, governance becomes embedded within it:

> “the organs of governance ‘stand in the midst of society’” and “governance and society are seen as cooperative rather than conflict-ridden, consultative rather than antagonistic” (Socialism_With_Chinese_Characteristics · Chapter 245).

So centralized state authority is portrayed as hierarchical domination, while the loss of public power’s political character is portrayed as a depoliticized, cooperative public power no longer standing above society as a coercive instrument.

She gives a double reason: inherited love and her own present feeling.

How does refusing to sell one's loyalty compare to a system where people themselves can be bought and sold?

Short answer: the Dune scene treats loyalty as precisely the thing that must not be a commodity, and the only "coin" that can win it is reciprocal, freely given commitment — whereas the Stalin text describes a historical sequence in which the person himself is the commodity: fully so under slavery, partially under feudalism, and formally freed but materially compelled under capitalism.

In the Arrakis scene, Kynes rejects the offer of a world's worth of trust as payment:

> "My loyalty’s not for sale, Sire." (Dune · Chapter 25)

Paul then reframes the transaction away from property entirely: "You say you’re not for sale, but I believe I’ve the coin you’ll accept. For your loyalty I offer my loyalty to you…totally." The bond is sealed as a personal, non-alienable one — "No Atreides has ever broken such a bond." (Dune · Chapter 25)

Stalin's sketch of the modes of production traces the opposite logic, where the person is what is owned and exchanged:

> "the slaveowner owns the means of production, he also owns the worker in production – the slave, whom he can sell, purchase, or kill as though he were an animal." (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · p. 24)

Under feudalism the ownership is partial — the lord "does not fully own the worker in production – the serf, whom the feudal lord can no longer kill, but whom he can buy and sell." Under capitalism the person is no longer sellable at all: the capitalist owns the means of production but "not the workers in production – the wage laborers, whom the capitalist can neither kill nor sell because they are personally free, but who are deprived of means of production and in order not to die of hunger, are obliged to sell their labor power to the capitalist and to bear the yoke of exploitation." (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · p. 25)

The contrast is sharp. In the Dune exchange, what circulates between Paul and Kynes is a bond between free parties that neither can convert into property — Kynes refuses the coin, and Paul wins him not by purchase but by pledging himself. In Stalin's schema, the direction of history is the widening of formal personal freedom, yet what the laborer must still sell is his labor power, because he is "deprived of means of production." So the seller of loyalty in Dune is the antithesis of the slave, serf, or wage-laborer: he is the one figure who cannot be owned at any stage of the sequence, and whose commitment, once given, is described as unbreakable rather than transferable.

When trying to reconnect with someone, does restoring full memory matter more, or does learning and teaching each other?

The evidence doesn’t set up an abstract ranking, but in these passages learning and teaching each other is shown as the real path of reconnection, while restoring full memory is presented as a coercive temptation.

In *Dune*, when Jessica and Stilgar begin to establish trust, Jessica says:

> “No doubt we have much to teach each other” (Dune · Chapter 31).

Stilgar replies:

> “This will be a good exchange of teachings” (Dune · Chapter 31).

He also frames correction as a gift:

> “To save one from a mistake is a gift of paradise” (Dune · Chapter 31).

By contrast, the offer to restore Chani with full memory in *Dune Messiah* is explicitly a Tleilaxu manipulation. Scytale says:

> “We can restore her to you. A ghola, Atreides. A ghola with full memory !” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 23).

Paul is tempted—“To hear Chani’s voice once more... To feel her presence beside me”—but refuses:

> “There are some prices an Atreides cannot pay” (Dune Messiah · Chapter 23).

So the material implies that mutual learning and teaching is the healthier, more authentic way to reconnect; full-memory restoration is treated as something that can be weaponized, not as the real work of relationship.

The implications are far-reaching: without political character based on class struggle, antagonistic struggle between different political parties would no longer exist, so much so that ‘elections have nothing [hat nichts] of today’s political character [politischen Charakter]’ (Marx 1875b, 635; 1875d, 519-520). To begin with, the matters of life and the economy can be managed for the benefit of society (Marx and Engels 1872b, 49-50; 1872a, 121; Engels 1894, 535; see also Wang and Wei 2017, 10). No longer functioning as “political footballs’ that can be tossed from one political party to another, with the one constantly seeking to undo the policies of the other, policies in all areas can be enacted in terms of ‘watching over the true interests of society’ (Engels 1873a, 86; 1873c, 425). As the Chinese translation of this text puts it, the purpose is to safeguard social interests and benefits—‘weihu zhenzheng shehui liyi’ (Engels 1873b, 338).° Further, instead of antagonism and conflict between state and society, the organs of governance ‘stand in the midst of society [steht eben mitten in der Gesellschaft]’ (Engels 1892a, 265; 1892b, 275)? The quotation comes from Engels’s detailed study of the comprehensive pre-state governing roles in The Origin of the Family, with their democratic councils, elected positions, and significant administrative functions. But the point here is that governance and society are seen as cooperative rather than conflict-ridden, consultative rather than antagonistic (Liu W. 2002). How are these pre-state forms of baseline democracy relevant for socialist democracy? The clearest answer may be found in 7See also the useful study by Jia Jianfang (2014, 3-6). 80r, as another Chinese term puts it, to “serve the community [gongtongti fuwu]’. Gongtongti is a word that arose in Chinese through the translation of the works of Engels and Marx, especially The German Ideology (Marx and Engels 1846). It is a rendering of Gemeinschaft and Gemeinwesen, but the fuwu (JR) is crucial, for it means to be in the service of society or the collective as whole (Boer and Zang 2019). °T quote here from the most widely used fourth and revised edition of 1892. The first edition of The Origin of the Family was published in 1884.

What does this commentary suggest a ruler truly needs to govern well?

**Sensitivity — not prophecy, not godhood, and not law or precedent — is what a ruler needs.** In this exchange Leto II tells Stilgar that good government rests on the ruler's own personal qualities rather than on institutions:

> "A ruler need not be a prophet, Stil. Nor even godlike. A ruler need only be sensitive. I brought you here with me to clarify what our Imperium requires. It requires good government. That does not depend upon laws or precedent, but upon the personal qualities of whoever governs." (Children of Dune · Chapter 17)

The passage builds a fuller picture of the ruler's required character:

- **Servanthood, not privilege.** Stilgar notes: "Naib has an ancient meaning... It is 'servant of the Sietch.'" Leto agrees that he is "expected to be Emperor, but I must be the servant," echoing his grandfather's motto, "Here I am; here I remain." (Children of Dune · Chapter 17)
- **Constant, tradition-rooted conduct.** Leto's conclusion is that he must "be constant, every action rooted in the traditions of the past," because "For proper government, the tribe must have ways to choose men whose lives reflect the way a government should behave." (Children of Dune · Chapter 17)
- **Self-control as the measure of fitness.** Under Fremen practice, Stilgar says, "You'll assume the Imperial Mantle if it's meet. First you must prove that you can behave in the fashion of a ruler!" — and that behaving with propriety regardless of inner desire "is the essence of self-control." (Children of Dune · Chapter 17)
- **Watchfulness about those around the throne.** Leto warns Stilgar, "If I die here, Stil... you must beware of Alia. She is no longer your friend." (Children of Dune · Chapter 17)

So the commentary's answer is that legitimacy comes from the ruler's lived character — sensitivity, service, constancy, and self-mastery — while prophecy, divinity, law, and precedent are explicitly rejected as the foundation. (Children of Dune · Chapter 17)

Dimela interrupted because Teg was briefing her as though she were a child who needed every instruction spelled out — she resented being handled that way and wanted to know what actually mattered: whether the assignment pulling him away was dangerous.

(2) Front/back matter (glossaries, appendices, terminology pages) is the library's own text — cite it like any source. (3) If the library does not contain it, state that limitation ONCE, then give
Why could a slave owner sell, buy, or even kill a slave?

**Because in the slave system the owner's property right covered the producer himself, not merely the means of production.** Stalin puts it directly: "the slave-owner owns the means of production, he also owns the worker in production – the slave, whom he can sell, purchase, or kill as though he were an animal" (Dialectical and Historical Materialism · p. 24).

The text gives three linked grounds:

1. **Ownership in the "full sense."** With the common ownership of the primitive commune gone, "Here, therefore, there is no common ownership of the means of production or of the fruits of production. It is replaced by private ownership. Here the slaveowner appears as the prime and principal property owner in the full sense of the term" (p. 24). Owning the slave as property is what makes sale, purchase and killing acts of a proprietor disposing of his own goods.

2. **Forced labour instead of free labour.** "Here we no longer find the common and free labor of all members of society in the production process – here there prevails the forced labor of slaves, who are exploited by the non-laboring slave-owners" (p. 24). Because the slave has no share and no personal holding, nothing restrains the master but his own interest.

3. **The class character of the system.** "Rich and poor, exploiters and exploited, people with full rights and people with no rights, and a fierce class struggle between them – such is the picture of the slave system" (p. 24).

The material precondition, per the same passage, was the new level of the productive forces — metal tools, pasturage, tillage, handicrafts, division of labour, and exchange — which created "the accumulation of wealth in the hands of a few... and the possibility of subjugation of the majority by a minority and the conversion of the majority into slaves" (p. 24).

**Context (not a library quote):** later slave law in various societies did restrict killing as a property right (Roman *lex Petronia*, for instance), so the text describes the classic slave relation in its pure form rather than every historical legal detail.

The commentary says the reliability of the apostolic message is confirmed by two things: the transfiguration of Jesus and the prophetic message.

Why did some enslaved people win their freedom by spying during the Revolutionary War?

Enslaved people won freedom through espionage chiefly because colonial and state legislatures rewarded valuable intelligence work with legislative emancipation — manumission granted as payment for service, sometimes with a pension added.

The evidence gives several concrete cases:

> "Rhode Island, in 1782, freed a Negro, Quaco Honeyman, as a reward for important spying activity; South Carolina, in 1783, freed the wife and child of a deceased Negro whose spying efforts had been valuable." (Aptheker, American Revolution · pp. 227–228)

> "Virginia, in 1786, freed James, slave of William Armistead, because he had, in 1781 at the seige of Yorktown, as the act of emancipation declares, entered 'into the service of the Marquis La Fayette, and at the peril of his life found means to frequent the British camp, and thereby faithfully executed important commissions entrusted to him by the Marquis.'" (Aptheker, American Revolution · pp. 227–228)

Note the mechanism in James's case: the emancipation was enacted by the Virginia legislature, and the rewards continued — "On liberation, James became James Lafayette; in 1819, the Virginia legislature awarded him $100, with an annual pension thereafter of $40." (Aptheker, American Revolution · p. 228) Earlier in the same passage an unnamed "Pompey" is likewise recorded as freed for his services.

Aptheker frames the deeper motive on the enslaved people's own side: their activities — including service "as pilots, seamen, laborers, soldiers, spies" — "always had as their fundamental motivation the achievement of freedom, the realization, in fullest practice, of the Declaration of Independence." (Aptheker, American Revolution · p. 228) In other words, spying was one of the few routes by which enslaved people could convert their indispensable knowledge of British and American movements into legal liberty, and the states' willingness to pay in freedom reflected both the military value of that intelligence and the Revolution's own emancipatory rhetoric.

Context-based note (not from the library): this was exceptional and piecemeal rather than a general policy — rewards went to individuals whose service commanders vouched for, and the vast majority of enslaved people gained nothing from such legislation.

How does knowing something intellectually differ from actually believing it or putting it into practice?

The one direct treatment of this distinction in the passages retrieved is in Herbert, where Leto draws the line sharply between intellectual assent and actual belief — and Moneo, challenged, defends himself by pleading the limits of what he can verify:

> "You know intellectually that even I will suffer a kind of death someday," Leto said. "But you do not believe it."
>
> "How can I believe what I will never see?" (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 8)

Moneo's reply is the crux: he can hold a proposition as true in the abstract — that Leto is mortal — yet not let it govern his expectations or conduct, because it lies outside anything he has seen or can test. Leto then presses the same point about risk and action rather than certainty: "You are right to observe that accidents happen even in my universe. Does this teach you nothing?" (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 8). Observation, even confident observation, isn't the same as having absorbed what it implies. Earlier in the same scene Leto also notes the gap from the other side — "Others have survived the test, Moneo. You did" (God Emperor of Dune · Chapter 8) — a lived experience that Moneo nonetheless cannot transfer to his fear for Siona, which again shows how poorly abstract knowledge moves a person compared to what has been undergone.

The retrieved Ibn Khaldun material (on wazirs, hājibs, doorkeepers and dynastic offices) does not address this question; I mention it only to confirm it was searched and bears on nothing here.

Beyond the evidence: the distinction is commonly framed as knowledge in the head versus knowledge in the bones — propositional assent that a thing is true, versus a conviction that actually reorganizes one's expectations and behavior. The first can coexist with contradicting conduct (someone who "knows" smoking kills but lights up); the second tends to collapse the distance between belief and act. What converts one into the other is usually, as in Moneo's case, experience: not more information but stakes — something lost, risked, or undergone that makes the proposition personal. That last paragraph is my own general framing, not something drawn from the library.

So: intellectually knowing is accepting a claim as true on the available grounds; believing, in the operative sense, is having it shape what you actually expect and do — and the text shows the two can sit side by side in the same person.

What were creditors sometimes obliged to accept as payment?

Creditors were at times obliged to accept barley as payment rather than payment in silver or another preferred medium.

The retrieved index entry reads:

> "obliged to accept barley for payment 140" (…and Forgive Them Their Debts · Chapter 43)

This appears in the book's index under **creditor**, alongside related entries such as "keeping pledges upon default 51," "family of debtor entered his house 112," "borrowing from individual 100," and "avoidance of debt cancelation 112." The cluster reflects the book's broader argument that ancient Near Eastern law and custom limited creditors' freedom to dictate the form of repayment and to seize collateral — protecting the debtor's subsistence and the community's viability.

That single index line is all the library evidence provides here; it does not, in the passages retrieved, spell out the legal reasoning behind the rule. My own context: this fits the well-documented Mesopotamian pattern in which barley (the staple crop and standard unit of account) functioned as legal tender for debts, so a creditor could not refuse it simply because he preferred silver or another commodity.

I recall Engels writing to Bebel about the “free people’s state” becoming a “free state”—what’s the complete quotation and its source?

Engels' remarks come from his letter to August Bebel of March 18–28, 1875, criticizing the draft Gotha Programme (the same draft Marx attacked in his letter to Bracke). Lenin quotes it in full:

> "The free people's state has been transferred into the free state. Taken in its grammatical sense, a free state is one where the state is free in relation to its citizens, hence a state with a despotic government. The whole talk about the state should be dropped, especially since the Commune, which was no longer a state in the proper sense of the word. The 'people's state' has been thrown in our faces by the anarchists to the point of disgust, although already Marx's book against Proudhon and later the Communist Manifesto say plainly that with the introduction of the socialist order of society the state dissolves of itself [sich auflost] and disappears. As the state is only a transitional institution which is used in the struggle, in the revolution, to hold down one's adversaries by force, it is sheer nonsense to talk of a 'free people's state'; so long as the proletariat still needs the state, it does not need it in the interests of freedom but in order to hold down its adversaries, and as soon as it becomes possible to speak of freedom the state as such ceases to exist. We would therefore propose replacing the state everywhere by Gemeinwesen, a good old German word which can very well take the place of the French word commune." (State and Revolution · Chapter IV: Supplementary Explanations by Engels)

Source details given in the same place: the letter is dated March 18–28, 1875; the passage is cited at pp. 321–22 of the German original, and the letter was first published by Bebel in the second volume of his memoirs, *Aus meinem Leben* (1911), 36 years after it was written (State and Revolution · Chapter IV: Supplementary Explanations by Engels).

Lenin adds that since Engels was then living with Marx in London and Marx's own letter to Bracke followed only weeks later (May 5, 1875), Engels' "we" in the final sentence speaks in Marx's name as well — suggesting the German workers' party strike the word "state" from its programme in favour of "community."

Note: the line you recall as "the free people's state has been transferred into the free state" appears in the evidence exactly as quoted above; some editions render it "has been transformed into the free state." The wording above is what this source gives.

How does uncovering the hidden, inner meanings of a sacred text compare with directly knowing another person’s private past?

The evidence suggests the two are only superficially similar: both disclose something concealed, but the method and purpose differ sharply.

For sacred text, hidden meaning is uncovered through a tradition of layered, interior interpretation. The Study Quran notes al-Simnānī’s coordination of “the levels of interior meaning mentioned in this ḥadīth with the seven subtle centers” (The Study Quran · p. 4065). In other words, exegesis is tied to spiritual states and contemplative faculties, not just factual retrieval.

For another person’s private past, the disclosed knowledge in *Heretics of Dune* is exact, verbatim, and tied to surveillance and breeding control. Odrade quotes Teg’s own past words: “I had never been out of the Sisterhood’s sight for an instant! I was never a free agent.” Teg reacts that “Odrade had them down as accurately as a mechanical recorder. Even the tone!” (Heretics of Dune · Chapter 14). She then reveals, “I am one of your daughters,” and explains, “The Sisterhood takes no chances that our genotype will be sent into the wild gene pool” (Heretics of Dune · Chapter 14). Teg recognizes the aim: “Manipulation. That was their mark. They manipulated everyone and everything” (Heretics of Dune · Chapter 14).

Thus, uncovering a sacred text’s inner meanings is portrayed as spiritual and interpretive, coordinated with interior centers; directly knowing a private past is portrayed as precise memory/intelligence used to demonstrate power, paternity, and the absence of free agency.

Why do humans need each other’s help to defend themselves against predatory animals?

Ibn Khaldūn's answer is that a lone human is physically outmatched by animals, and the artificial "limbs" that compensate — weapons — cannot be made or used by one person alone.

> "The power of one individual human being cannot withstand the power of any one dumb animal, especially the power of the predatory animals. Man is generally unable to defend himself against them by himself. Nor is his unaided power sufficient to make use of the existing instruments of defence, because there are so many of them and they require so many crafts and things. It is absolutely necessary for man to have the co-operation of his fellow men." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1, "Human Civilization in General")

His underlying premise is that nature gave humans no built-in defences; crafts supply substitutes for the organs other animals possess:

> "Lances, for instance, take the place of horns for goring, swords the place of claws to inflict wounds, shields the place of thick skins, and so on." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1)

The consequence of isolation is spelled out: without co-operation man "cannot obtain any food or nourishment, and life cannot materialize for him," and "he falls prey to animals and dies much before his time," so that "the human species would vanish" (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1). With mutual co-operation, by contrast, "man obtains food for his nourishment and weapons for his defence."

Two further points from the same passage are worth keeping distinct:

- **Crafts as the mediating factor.** Weapons exist only as products of many crafts, and those crafts require many hands — this is why the argument is not simply about numbers of bodies but about division of labour.
- **The limit of the remedy.** These weapons, made for defence "against the aggressiveness of dumb animals," are expressly said *not* to suffice against human aggression, "because all of them possess those weapons" — which is why a restraining authority (royal authority) is separately required (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 1).

So the need for help is twofold in Khaldūn: co-operation is required to *produce and wield* defensive instruments, and, once produced, those instruments leave humans as exposed to one another as they were to beasts.

What inner quality set Ibn Khaldûn apart and made his masterpiece possible?

The distinguishing inner quality was an imaginative mobility — the ability to see his own world from an outsider's vantage point, which the 2005 introduction calls the "critical element" behind the Muqaddimah:

> "What made Ibn Khaldûn different was not travel per se but rather his ability to travel in the imagination of his own world, to create another perspective that at once linked him to his contemporaries yet set him apart from them. Whether we call this disposition quirkiness or eccentricity, narcissism or genius, we must recognize it as the critical element of Ibn Khaldûn that made it possible for him to conceive, then write the Muqaddimah" (The Muqaddimah · Introduction, 2005 edition).

The same introduction stresses that this difference was "almost reflexive" and expressed itself in outward marks as well as thought — his dress, for instance: as a judge in Cairo he kept wearing Maghribi (North African) robes rather than the lighter robes of Egyptian judges, signalling "pride in his Andalusian roots." It also notes he was "a juridical activist with a secondary interest in history," who looked in his own experience for lessons (*'ibar*) instructive to others (The Muqaddimah · Introduction, 2005 edition).

Context (not from the library text): historians conventionally frame this as Ibn Khaldûn's sociological imagination — the detachment that let him theorize group solidarity (*'asabiyya*) and the rise-and-decline cycle of dynasties rather than merely chronicle events. The quoted introduction itself declines to settle whether the trait is "quirkiness or eccentricity, narcissism or genius," treating the label as less important than the capacity.

The clearest statement of water-as-wealth comes in Jessica's reaction:

How do bodily pain and distrust of authority each make a person feel separate from those around them?

**Short answer:** In both passages, pain and suspicion work the same way — each turns other people from companions into something unreachable. Pain collapses the self to a single burning thread so that "other presences" are only noise; suspicion converts others into tools or threats, so that shared life becomes a technique for survival rather than fellowship.

**Bodily pain (Murbella's Agony):** Pain narrows her world to herself and simultaneously severs her from the crowd around her. Her embodiment thins to almost nothing:

> "Her sense of presence in living flesh became a thin thread that wound through many presences. She sensed others all around her, far too many people for the tiny amphitheater." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 35)

Others exist, but only as raw proximity, and the collective voice she hears is not comfort:

> "Persistent wailing came from the other presences. Laments: 'See? See what happens when you ignore common sense?'" (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 35)

Even Duncan's touch, the one connection that reaches her, arrives as pain rather than contact: "Murbella felt a familiar hand on her cheek. Duncan! The touch restored agony" (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 35). The world contracts further until she is nothing but the sensation:

> "The thread no longer was stretching. It was pulling back, compressing. It became one small thing, a sausage of such exquisite pain that nothing else existed." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 35)

Pain therefore separates by *reduction*: many presences around her, but only one thing that exists — her own agony.

**Distrust of authority (Halleck):** Halleck's suspicion of Alia's Regency isolates him socially by making every relationship instrumental. He concludes:

> "I can't trust them, Halleck thought. He could only use them and nurture their distrust of others. It was sad. Gone was the old give and take of free men." (Children of Dune · Chapter 56)

Distrust also makes him hear betrayal in ordinary speech — "And Halleck heard the sly dissimulation in the man's voice. What that voice revealed told Halleck there was sanctuary here for only a limited time" (Children of Dune · Chapter 56) — so even hospitality is read as a countdown, and his plan is "Just until I can steal one of their 'thopters" (Children of Dune · Chapter 56). Where pain isolates by compressing the self, distrust isolates by hollowing out community: the "old ways" survive only as dead ritual.

**The common thread:** both conditions dissolve the middle ground between self and others — for Murbella, others become unreachable presences; for Halleck, others become usable or treacherous ones.
