Register:
What does the commentary claim were the reasons Britain agreed to such favorable boundary terms for the Americans?

Aptheker's commentary lists six mutually reinforcing reasons, explicitly as his own argument ("We think there were six major considerations"):

> "First stands the fact that after fighting from 1775 through 1781 the British were further than ever from having subdued the Americans. Again, by the time the diplomatic groundwork for peace with the Americans was being laid, Great Britain found herself in an exceedingly isolated and disadvantageous position in the European power game. Third, by the early 1780's the majority of all classes of Englishmen were insisting that peace be made and on that basis the North Government had been forced to resign. Fourth, there was a very strong desire among the Whigs who succeeded North to salvage something from the Tory wreckage by developing a policy which would win American friendship. Fifth, there was great anxiety in the British Foreign Office that America be drawn out of the orbit of French influence and, if possible, that enmity between France and the United States be developed. And sixth, the Treaty of 1783 came as the British Government was replacing its whole original conception of colonialism from one which stressed English conquest and settlement to one which stressed English conquest and penetration and domination, but not settlement." (Aptheker, American Revolution · Chapter VIII, p. 203)

In brief, the six are: (1) military failure to subdue the Americans; (2) Britain's isolation in European power politics; (3) domestic insistence on peace, which brought down the North ministry; (4) Whig desire to win American friendship; (5) Foreign Office hope of detaching America from France and fostering Franco-American enmity; (6) a shift in the British conception of colonialism toward conquest and penetration rather than settlement.

The section is framed against a prior point in the same commentary: although the Foreign Office knew American minimum and maximum demands and internal divisions, "there is no available evidence demonstrating that such knowledge actually determined any feature of the final Treaty" (Aptheker, American Revolution · Chapter VIII, p. 202) — so the six reasons, not British intelligence about American negotiating positions, carry the explanatory weight. Aptheker also credits the American side to "three distinguished men who complemented each other extremely well: Franklin, John Adams and John Jay" (Aptheker, American Revolution · Chapter VIII, p. 203), with Franklin in particular reminding British plenipotentiary David Hartley of his past advocacy for the American cause.

[Library-based: all quotations above. No outside knowledge needed to answer; general historical literature on the Treaty of 1783 is not drawn on here.]

According to the commentary, why does Chani push for Irulan to bear Paul’s child?

Chani pushes for Irulan to bear Paul's child for two intertwined reasons: dynastic necessity and political calculation — plus a Fremen cultural logic that an heir is not left to one woman's fate.

The dynastic motive is explicit. Chani has not conceived, and in her mind that means someone else must:

> "You must have an heir!" she husked. (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3)

> So that was it: Chani had not produced a child for him. Someone else, then, must do it. Why not Irulan? That was the way Chani's mind worked. (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3)

> "An heir to House Atreides, this is not something you leave to chance or one woman." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3)

The political motive is that an Atreides pregnancy would compromise Irulan with the conspirators around her:

> "If she carried an Atreides child, her friends would question her loyalties. The less trust our enemies place in her, the less use she is to them." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3)

Note that Chani frames this as concern for Paul, not for Irulan: "It's concern for you, not for her!" (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3). Paul resists, warning of the danger it poses to Chani — "A child for her could mean your death," Paul said. "You know the plotting in this place." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3) — and insists, "You'll give me the only heir I want." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3)

The cultural background is Fremen: "Fremen women had shared their men for thousands of years—not always in peace, but with a way of making the fact nondestructive. Something mysteriously Fremen in this fashion had happened in Chani." (Dune Messiah · Chapter 3)

So the commentary's answer: Chani wants an heir secured for House Atreides rather than risked on her alone, and simultaneously wants a child by Irulan to erode Irulan's usefulness to Paul's enemies — a decision Paul reads as "an act of love" made on Fremen terms, against his own veto.

What does the commentary say about the arguments over naming the Congress’s presiding officer and secretary?

This is a definition/commentary question, so the relevant passage is in the actual text.

The commentary — Aptheker's account of the First Continental Congress's organizational phase — makes the point that even these procedural/technical disputes were factional contests between the Left and the Right. On the naming of the body itself:

> "have a name more high-sounding than that of the purely func-tional term, 'The Congress'; but the simplicity seemed a virtue to the Left, and Congress it remained." (American Revolution · "The Development of Revolutionary Institutions")

On the presiding officer, the Right wanted a grander title:

> "The Right strongly urged that the Congress presiding officer, selected by the delegates, have a name in keeping with the traditions of prominence, such as His Eminence, or His Majesty, or the like. The Left thought the chosen presiding officer was simply the President and that that title would go very well with the Congress, and 'the President' it was." (American Revolution · "The Development of Revolutionary Institutions")

On the secretary, the fight was over persons, not titles:

> "Particularly heated, in the organizational phase of the First Congress' meeting, was the question of who was to serve as its Secretary. Joseph Galloway supported a conservative Connecticut lawyer, Silas Deane, for the post, while the Left wished to appoint Charles Thomson, though not a delegate, for he was the outstanding mass leader of Philadelphia. Thomson it was, and he held the post until 1789 when the Congress formed by the new Constitution came into being." (American Revolution · "The Development of Revolutionary Institutions")

Aptheker's interpretive conclusion ties these to the larger conflict:

> "These defeats of the Right on rather technical questions heralded its defeat on the major substantive questions before the body." (American Revolution · "The Development of Revolutionary Institutions")

Context (my own summary, not library text): the Left won both the title and the secretaryship — a plain "President" rather than an honorific, and Thomson over Deane — which Aptheker treats as a preview of the Left's victories on substantive matters, notably the rejection of Galloway's plan of union and the approval of the Suffolk Resolves.

Why was it difficult for Brian Herbert to understand his father while growing up?

Brian Herbert says it was his father's single-minded devotion to writing — and his own childhood jealousy of the fictional characters — that made Frank Herbert hard to understand. In his afterword he writes:

> "Growing up in Frank Herbert's household, I did not understand his need for absolute silence so that he could concentrate, the intense desire he had to complete his important writing projects, or the confidence he had that one day his writing would be a success, despite the steady stream of rejections that he received." (Dune · Chapter 63)

He adds that the characters came between them:

> "To my young eyes, the characters he created in Dune and his other stories were the children of his mind, and they competed with me for his affections. In the years it took him to write his magnum opus, he spent more time with Paul Atreides than he did with me. Dad's study was off-limits to me, to my sister Penny, and to my brother Bruce. In those days, only my mother Beverly really understood Dad's complexities." (Dune · Chapter 63)

So the difficulty was threefold: a father who required "absolute silence" and a closed study; a young son who felt rivaled by Paul Atreides for his father's attention; and no one in the house able to interpret him except Beverly Herbert. Brian adds that he spent years "having rebelled against his exacting ways," and that it was only in his "mid-twenties," after seeing how Frank cared for his dying mother, that "he and I became the best of friends" (Dune · Chapter 63).

That is the whole of the library's evidence on the question; the passage is Brian's own retrospective account, not an outside historian's judgment.

According to the commentary, how deeply has Muad'Dib's religious mythos penetrated ordinary human life?

Muad'Dib's mythos has saturated the most elementary, everyday acts — eating, sex, birth, even walking and building:

> "I've had a bellyful of the god and priest business! You think I don't see my own mythos? Consult your data once more, Hayt. I've insinuated my rites into the most elementary human acts. The people eat in the name of Muad'Dib! They make love in my name, are born in my name—cross the street in my name. A roof beam cannot be raised in the lowliest hovel of far Gangishree without invoking the blessing of Muad'Dib!" (Dune Messiah · Chapter 13)

The speaker — Paul-Muad'Dib himself, in the excerpt from the BOOK OF DIATRIBES as recorded in the HAYT CHRONICLE — frames this as an accusation against himself: the religion is not confined to temple ritual but has been "insinuated" into ordinary life so thoroughly that no act, however private or trivial, escapes it. Note especially the sweep of the claim: it reaches from the most intimate (lovemaking, childbirth) to the most mundane (crossing a street) and to the humblest social scale — "the lowliest hovel of far Gangishree," a place otherwise insignificant, still cannot raise a roof beam without invoking his blessing. That is the measure of penetration: universality across class, geography, and the entire range of human activity, with Paul noting bitterly that he sees his own mythos with clear eyes. Nothing in the retrieved passage goes beyond this; it is commentary spoken in Paul's own voice rather than a systematic theological definition.

Why can’t a husband treat multiple wives with perfect equality?

The Quran's own answer, as the commentary explains it, is that such perfect equality is humanly impossible: "V. 129 states that men will never be able to deal equitably between their wives, even if they desire to do so" (The Study Quran · 4:129c).

The commentary then situates this within the wider justice theme of the passage: "Some have asserted that although treating one's wives equally is an ideal one should strive for, lack of perfection in this regard does not itself nullify the legitimacy of polygamous marriage (see 4:129c). This whole verse revolves around the issue of justice; it favors neither polygamy nor monogamy absolutely and advises the form that best facilitates the just treatment of orphans, wives, and other dependents" (The Study Quran · 4:3c).

It also defines what "dealing justly" covers: "Dealing justly between one's wives means treating them equitably with regard to financial support, love, companionship, and conjugal relations (Q)" (The Study Quran · 4:3c). Since love and companionship are named among the things equity must cover, the impossibility stated in 4:129 is the impossibility of perfectly evening out inward affection and attachment, not merely material provision.

**Context / general knowledge (not a library quotation):** classical exegesis typically distinguishes the *outward, measurable* obligations — maintenance, housing, nights spent with each wife — which a husband is commanded to keep equal and can in principle do, from *inward* matters — love, desire, and the feelings of the heart — which are outside a person's volitional control and for which, on this reading, he is not blamed. The verse's "even if you desire to do so" is precisely the acknowledgement that the obstacle is not unwillingness but the limits of human capacity. Both scales appear in the evidence — and Herbert links them. Suspicion does not choose between private love and public power; it corrodes the intimate bond and hardens the ruler's hand at once.

**The loved one, made strange.** In *Chapterhouse*, Duncan's wariness of Murbella is not estrangement but a mutation of intimacy:

The wound is precisely that openness: "'Don't hate me, Duncan.' No pleading but something deeply hurt behind the words." / "'I'll never hate you.' But he turned off the light." **Suspicion aimed back at him.** Duncan is also the watched party. Odrade's dream-voice states the terms plainly: "I make decisions of necessity, Duncan. Little likelihood you'll break out and run amok." (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 36). Waking, he finds a design in his head and asks, "How was that smuggled into my mind?" — then, "Influencing my dreams? What have I tapped?" (Chapterhouse Dune · Chapter 36). A leader's grip and a lover's distrust share one mechanism: the other person becomes a possible instrument.

**The tightening grip.** *Children of Dune* shows the ruler's version. Farad'n answers his advisor's protest with compulsion: "'Later, I said!' For the first time, he used Voice on Tyekanik, saw the man blink with surprise and remain silent." Jessica's response is telling: "A tight smile touched Jessica's mouth." (Children of Dune · Chapter 63). Ghanima supplies the philosophy sustaining such a grip — power exercised through a "cult of death," because "It's a tension by which the living know they're alive," closing with "We always arise from our own ashes. Always." (Children of Dune · Chapter 63).

So: dislike of a loved one and a leader's clenched authority are two faces of the same suspicion — the belief that the trusted other may not be what they seem, and must therefore be managed.

Why should remembering God be spoken quietly rather than silently?

The key point is that the invocation was to be **audible to oneself** — a low voice, not silence — so that the bodily act of speech could work back on the inner faculties and strengthen remembrance in the heart:

> "the invocation or remembrance enjoined here should be done not silently, but in a voice low enough that it can be heard only by oneself, since there is a profound connection between the body, soul, and spirit—each of which is a door to the others—a connection that is activated by the process of remembering or invoking God. Hearing the invocation uttered by the bodily tongue moves the imagination and soul of the one invoking, which in turn strengthens the remembrance in the spiritual heart. The act of remembrance thus takes place simultaneously on all three levels, each reflecting upon and strengthening the others." (The Study Quran · commentary preceding verse 206, p. 1023)

The same passage notes that some read the quietness injunction as a prohibition of loud communal *dhikr* by Sufi groups, and that Ibn ʿAjībah rejects this, since the verse was revealed in Makkah "when the believers had to be circumspect in their worship, and … when the community migrated to Madinah, the Prophet and Companions would conduct public dhikr sessions in the mosque" (The Study Quran · commentary preceding verse 206, p. 1023).

The morning and evening are named as times especially suited to remembrance, and also, according to the commentators cited there, as a way of saying one should remember and praise God at all times, the two times symbolizing "transition between light and darkness, sleeping and waking, and thus suggestive of death and resurrection" (The Study Quran · commentary preceding verse 206, p. 1023).

**Context/outside note:** this is the standard Sufi psychology of *dhikr* — the tongue's movement is not the goal but the trigger that engages imagination, soul, and heart together; hence the recommendation of a "secret" or whispered remembrance rather than either full silence or loud recitation.

Why can leadership over a people only belong to someone who shares their descent?

**Short answer (Ibn Khaldūn's own argument):** because leadership rests on superiority, superiority rests on group feeling (ʿaṣabiyya), and the only secure source of group feeling is common descent — so a mere client or ally, attached to a tribe but not sharing its descent, cannot legitimately lead it.

The core syllogism:

> "This is because leadership exists only through superiority, and superiority only through group feeling. Leadership over people, therefore, must, of necessity, derive from a group feeling that is superior to each individual group feeling. Each individual group feeling that becomes aware of the superiority of the group feeling of the leader is ready to obey and follow him." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 2)

The outsider's defect is that attachment is not kinship:

> "Now, a person who has become attached to people of a common descent usually does not share the group feeling that derives from their common descent. He is merely attached to them. The firmest connection he has with the group is as client and ally. This in no way guarantees him superiority over them." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 2)

Hence leadership is inherited only within the line marked for superiority:

> "Leadership must of necessity be inherited from the person who is entitled to it, in accordance with the fact, which we have stated, that superiority results from group feeling." (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 2)

The companion point explains why fabricated pedigrees are self-defeating: a leader who grafts himself onto another descent "bring[s] suspicion upon themselves with regard to their leadership and nobility" (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 2), since group feeling, not claimed ancestry, is the real currency. Nobility follows the same rule:

> "Only those who share in a group feeling can have a 'house' and nobility in the basic sense and in reality, while others have it only in a metaphorical and figurative sense" (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 2)

and city-dwellers can claim a "house" only metaphorically, "because there exists in this case a number of successive ancestors who consistently performed good deeds. This is not true and unqualified prestige" (The Muqaddimah · Chapter 2).

**Context/commentary (my own words, not a library quotation):** this is Khaldūn's sociology of ʿaṣabiyya — group solidarity generated by shared blood, which makes mutual aid and obedience reliable. Modern readers treat the descent claim as an ideal-type rather than a universal law: shared religion, patronage, or a warrior elite's corporate identity can also generate the cohesion he attributes to lineage.
